The Austrian Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador H. Winkler, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3, the Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was accused of threatening police officers by threatening them with job-related troubles in case they charged him with traffic offences. The case was brought by the Vienna Federal Police Directorate (Bundespolizeidirektion) to question the police officers involved in the traffic control at issue by way of letters rogatory. The Investigating Commissioner’s report was submitted to the Disciplinary Council on 3 June 1996. The applicant, his spouse and the two police officers were summoned for a hearing on 14 October 1996. But the hearing was cancelled as the applicant and his spouse could not appear at that date. The case was then adjourned and the applicant challenged the chairman and another member of the Dis disciplinary Council for bias. In February 1998, since the file at issue had meanwhile been transmitted to an other administrative authority, the Disdisciplinary Council filed a appeal to the Constitutional Court. The Disciplinary Council found that the applicant had misbehaved towards intervening police officers by threatening them with job-related troubles in case they charged him with traffic offences. The applicant was also ordered to pay an additional fine of ATS 10,000 as he had already been ordered to. to pay ATS 25,000 in four other sets of disciplinary proceedings. He lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) about the length of the proceedings and claimed that the disciplinary authorities had failed to take the excessive length of. the proceedings into account as a mitigating circumstance. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint on 29 February 2000.

On 14 June 2001 the Supreme Administrative Council upheld the decision of the Administrative Council. They were then taken into custody and released the next day. The case was transferred to the Ad Istanbul Provincial Administrative Council, seeking authorisation to bring criminal proceedings against the accused officers. In the meantime, on 1 June 1999 the Ad Turkey Public Prosecutor delivered a decision not to prosecute with regard to seventy demonstrators – including the applicants – who had been involved in the incident. The police were under an obligation to warn the group out loud to disperse. However, it was observed from the recording of the incident that they had failed to do so. In consequence, the public prosecutor held that the accused had not violated Law no. 2911. the Assemblies and Marches Act (Law no.2911), the police were found not to have violated the law. The case was settled out of court on a technicality, and the case was dismissed by the court of appeal. The incident occurred in the early hours of January 26, 2013. The council ordered disciplinary proceedings against her on the ground that she had failed to comply with the duty of loyalty to the Constitution. Mrs Vogt was found guilty of misconduct. She was suspended from her job and ordered to pay back the money she had lost as a result of the investigation. She also lost her job as a teacher at a secondary school in the Land of Hesse.

She had, it was said, engaged in various political activities on behalf of the DKP since the autumn of 1980.

It originated in an application (no. 17851/91) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a German national, Mrs Dorothea Vogt, on 13 February 1991. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention and also, in the case of the Commission's request, of Article 14. The Government sought leave to submit an additional memorial and requested that the hearing initially set down for 23 November be postponed. Mr Ryssdal granted these requests. On 26 January 1995 the Chamber decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of a Grand Chamber. The Grand Chamber comprised as ex officio members the President and the Vice-President, Mr Bernhardt, who in this case was already sitting as national judge. The names of the remaining ten judges were drawn by lot by the President in the presence of the Registrar on 27 January 1995. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 February 1995. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr Mr Bigi, Mr A.N. Loizou, Mr M.A. Lopes Rocha, Mr D. Gotchev and Mr P. Kuris. Mrs Dorothea Vogt, a German national born in 1949, lives in Jever in the Land of Lower Saxony. She studied literature and languages at the University of Marburg/Lahn for six years. In November 1975 she sat the examination to become a secondary-school teacher (wissenschaftliche Prüfung für das Lehramt an Gymnasien). She did her teaching practice from February 1976 to June 1977 at Fulda in theLand of Hesse. On 1 February 1979, before the end of her probationary period, she was appointed a permanent civil servant. In an assessment report drawn up in March 1981 her capabilities and work were described as entirely satisfactory. After a preliminary investigation, the Weser-Ems regional council issued an order (Verfügung) on 13 July 1982 instituting disciplinary proceedings against the applicant. She had, it was said, engaged in various political activities on behalf of the DKP since the autumn of 1980. The proceedings were stayed on 15 July 1985 in order to widen the investigations to include further instances of the applicant's political activity that had come to light in the meantime. Mrs Vogt was accused of also failing to comply with her duties as a civil servant in that she had been a member of the “Executive Committee’ (Vorstand) of the Bremen/North Lower Saxony regional branch. From October 1986 Mrs Vogt was paid only 60 per cent of her salary (Dienstbezüge) The applicant, who by her own account has been a member of the DKP since 1972, argued that her conduct could not amount to a failure to fulfil her duties as a civil servant. She had always carried out such activity within the law and within the limits laid down in the Constitution. Her action to promote peace within the Federal Republic of Germany and in its external relations and her combat against neo-fascism were in no way indicative of an anti-constitutional stance. The DKP's aims had always been wrongly alleged (but never proven) to be anti- constitutional. In its judgment of 15 October 1987 the Disciplinary Division dismissed applications by Mrs Vogt to have the proceedings stayed and witnesses examined. It considered that active membership of a political party that pursued anti-constitutional aims was incompatible with a civil servant's duty of political loyalty. It granted her a sum equivalent to 75 per cent of her pension entitlement at that date, to be paid for a six-month period. The Disciplinary division found in the first place that neither ILO Convention No. 111 nor the recommendations made in the Commission of Inquiry's report of 20 February 1987 constituted a bar to the opening of disciplinary proceedings. The DKP's aims, as described in the Mannheim programme of 21 October 1978 (see paragraph 22 below), were clearly opposed to the free democratic constitutional system of the Federal Republic of Germany. Duty of political loyalty was one of the traditional principles of the civil service and had constitutional status by virtue of Article 33 para. 5 of the Basic Law. This rule did not apply to measures, such as disciplinary proceedings, which initially had a different purpose and restricted the freedom to stand for election to, and to sit as a member of, parliament only as an indirect and unavoidable consequence of their implementation. The applicant had carried out her political activities despite being familiar with the case-law establishing that active membership of the DKP was incompatible with the duty of political Loyalty. She must have been aware, at the latest once the Lower Saxony Disciplinary Court (Niedersächsischer Disziplinarhof) had delivered its judgment of 24 June 1985. Civil servants must unequivocally dissociate themselves from groups who criticise, campaign against and cast aspersions on the State, its institutions and the existing constitutional system. As a result of her activities as a member of the DKP the applicant had failed to satisfy these requirements. The DKP's political aims were incompatible with that system. The court held that the applicant's reference to Article 5 para. 1 of the Basic Law, which secured the right to freedom of expression, was not relevant as the provisions governing the civil service mentioned in Article 33 para. 5 of the Civil Service Act were more relevant. Even though Mrs Vogt sought above all to support the constitutional system, she necessarily espoused anti-constitutional aims and had therefore to be considered to be opposed to the Constitution. The DKP's aims were admittedly not all anti-constitutional; some of them were compatible with the Basic Law. However, civil servants could not, as a means of furthering their own political objectives, make use of a party with anti- constitutional aims and help it to come to power. The former Communist Party (KPD) employed the 'tactics of conflict' employed by the former KPD but also the different phases of the process leading to attainment of its final objective of 'socialist rule' (BVerfGE 5, p. 85), the Federal Constitutional Court held. It also stated that intensive propaganda and persistent unrest aimed at establishing - even if this was not to be achieved in the near future - a 'proletarian revolution' The court also considered that the applicant's commitment to changing the DKP's policies could not exculpate her. The political loyalty owed by civil servants entailed a duty for them to dissociate themselves unequivocally from groups which criticised or cast aspersions on the State and the existing constitutional system. Parents, who because of compulsory education had to send their children to State schools, were entitled to expect the State to rely on its servants' loyalty to the Constitution. The court added that such a breach of duty was especially serious in the case of a teacher, who was supposed to teach the children entrusted to her care. Her dismissal had therefore been justified. The applicant lodged a constitutional complaint (Verfassungsbeschwerde) with the Federal Constitutional Court. The court decided on 7 August 1990 not to entertain the constitutional complaint, on the ground that it had insufficient prospects of success. The disciplinary tribunals had been entitled to find that the DKP's aims were anti-constitutional, notwithstanding the provisions of Article 21 para. 2 of the Basic Law. The applicant's dismissal had therefore not amounted to a breach of the principle of proportionality as regards her constitutional rights. Accordingly, there had been no violation of Article 33 paras. 2, 3 and 4 of the German constitution. From 1987 to 1991 the applicant worked as a playwright and drama teacher at the North Lower Saxony regional theatre (Landesbühne) in Wilhelmshaven. In 1991 she was reinstated in her post as a teacher for the LowerSaxony education authority. The Land government had beforehand repealed the decree on the employment of extremists in the Lower Saxonic civil service. By a decision of 3 June 2008, the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the lack of an oral Hearings to the Government. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1) The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Stockholm, claiming that his injuries had been caused by his work in Sweden. The Office requested the opinion of one of its own medical doctors (försäkringsläkare), Dr S.H., as to whether the applicant’s injuries were work-related. The doctor, who was a specialist in orthopaedics, gave his opinion on 23 September 1997. It was based on the information in the case-file and stated essentially the following. It appeared from other medical certificates that the applicant had been healthy until his hip joint problems began in 1985-86. In 1988 his right hip and lower back had been x-rayed, which showed that the hip joint had degenerative alterations. The applicant had a hip operation in July 1996 after suffering from arthritis in his right hip. He appealed to the County Administrative Court, maintaining that he was entitled to occupational injury compensation due to his injuries, which were clearly work-related. The Office disputed the appeal and submitted that Dr P.H.’s opinion did not clearly show that the applicant's work at the slaughterhouse had caused his injuries. The applicant renewed his request for an oral hearing but sent on the same day a fax to the court explaining that he did not request an oral Hearings. On 29 June 1999 the County administrative court rejected the applicant’S appeal. It did not question that his work had caused the injuries. The court found that the applicant had failed to show that there was a high level of probability that his work at the slaughterhouse had caused his hip joint arthritis. However, it noted that it had to be relatively widely accepted that certain factors in the working environment could cause the relevant injuries. The court granted the applicant two weeks to finalise his submissions in the case. The Administrative Court of Appeal rejected the appeal on 24 September 2001, and the case has now been adjourned until the end of the year. The applicant has appealed to the Swedish Court of Human Rights. The case has been referred to by the Human Rights Commission as the ‘Swedish Case’. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten) and requested that an oral hearing be held. He stressed that the lower courts had failed to hold a hearing, despite his express request and in violation of Article 6 of the Convention. The court rejected the applicant’s request as it considered that there was no need for a hearing before it decided on whether or not to grant leave to appeal. It gave the applicant three weeks to submit any additional comments. On 10 November 2003, the court refused the applicant's request for an appeal. The case was settled out of court and the applicant was awarded the right to appeal against the decision.

Mance LJ did not accept that the definition of torture in Article 1 of the Convention against Torture was fatal to the applicants’ claims. He did not consider it significant that Lieutenant Colonel Abdul Aziz had been described in Mr Jones’s claim as the “servant or agent” of Saudi Arabia. He noted that the House of Lords in Pinochet (No. 3) had considered that there would be no immunity from criminal prosecution in respect of an individual officer who had committed torture abroad in an official context. It was not easy to see why civil proceedings against an alleged torturer could be said to involve a greater interference in the internal affairs of a foreign State than criminal proceedings against the same person.

Mance LJ considered the case-law of the domestic courts and courts of other jurisdictions, which recognised State immunity ratione materiae in respect of acts of agents of the State. He noted that none of these cases was concerned with conduct which was to be regarded as outside the scope of any proper exercise of sovereign authority or with international crime. He did not accept that the definition of torture in Article 1 of the Convention against Torture as an act “by or at the instigation of or with the consent or acquiescence of a public official or other person acting in an official capacity” was fatal to the applicants’ claims.

The Polish Government were represented by their Agents, Mr Krzysztof Drzewicki and, subsequently, by Jakub Wołąsiewicz. On 10 November 1994 the Gdańsk Regional Court prolonged the applicant’s detention on remand until 21 January 1995. The court pointed out that the investigation had not yet been completed and that the group the applicant belonged to had brought improper pressure upon the witnesses to change their testimony. On 21 November 1994 an expert opinion on the state of the applicant's mental health was issued. On 5 April 1995 the applicant was ordered to undergo psychiatric observation. On 12 April 1995 he was released on bail and his case was adjourned until 30 June 1995. He has since been on bail awaiting trial for the murder of a Polish woman. The bill of indictment was lodged with the Gdańsk Regional Court against the applicant and eleven co-accused. Appeal upheld it, referring to the seriousness of the offence in question and the complexity of the case. He served his sentence between 15 March 1996 and 11 September 1997. The court dismissed the applicant’s request for release, considering that his case did not disclose any of the grounds for release provided by Article 218 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In a separate set of criminal proceedings, the applicant was sentenced by the Elbląg Regional Court to two and a half years imprisonment and a fine. Gdańsk Regional Court requested the Supreme Court to prolong the applicant’s detention until 30 June 1997. The Supreme Court granted the request on 16 January 1997. On 26 June 1997 the Regional Court lodged a request to prolong his detention until 31 December 1997. However, the limit of the duration of the detention was set at 1 December 1997 and not at 31 December 1996 as requested. The hearing scheduled for 25 September 1997 was adjourned as one of the hearings scheduled on 19 February 1997, 5 March 1997, 16 April 1997 and 11 June 1997 had been adjourned or cancelled because of the illnesses of the accused and the defending counsel. The Gdańsk Regional Court requested the Supreme Court to prolong the applicant’s detention on remand until 30 April 1998. The Supreme Court observed that a number of hearings had not been held due to the absence of either the co-accused or their defence counsel. The case was complex and multi-layered and the charges of a serious nature. In these circumstances, even though the proceedings in the case had been lengthy, the Regional Court could not be held responsible for this delay. On 22 October 2002 the court gave a judgment by which the applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two German nationals, Mr Ingo Hentschel and Mr Matthias Stark. On 9 December 2007 both applicants went to a football match in Munich. The police had predicted an increased risk of clashes between rival football supporters owing to confrontations at previous matches between the two teams. A total of 227 police officers were deployed, including two squads – comprising eight to ten police officers each – of the Munich riot control unit (Unterstützungskommando) and the 6th Dachau public-order support force battalion (Bereitschaftspolizei) Police cordoned off the stands of the supporters of one of the teams, including both applicants, to prevent them from leaving the stadium and encountering supporters of the other team. Both applicants were able to identify their attackers as police officers, but were not able to distinguish them further, owing to their identical uniforms and the lack of identifying signs or name tags. Both uniforms did not include any name tags or other signs identifying the individual officers. However, on the back of the helmets an identification number of the squad was displayed. The Government’s version of the subsequent events resulted in the arrest of one supporter and two police officers sustained minor injuries. Munich public prosecutor’s office instigated a preliminary investigation into alleged police violence. The Government challenged the accounts of the applicants and submitted that there was no credible evidence that the applicants had deliberately been hit or harmed by police officers. On 10 September 2008 the competent public prosecutor discontinued the investigation. He found that the investigation had produced evidence that some of the police officers had used truncheons against spectators, including women and children, in a disproportionate way and without an official order or approval. However, he concluded that the. investigation had not led to a situation where concrete acts of violence could be related to specific police. officers. The investigating division was also provided with a DVD showing excerpts of the video surveillance recorded by the riot control police at the match. The applicants appealed against the decision to discontinue the investigation. On 14 October 2008 the public prosecutor reopened the investigation and ordered further enquiries. Subsequently, a further twenty-two witnesses were interviewed including fourteen platoon leaders, squad leaders and video officers of the deployed police units. The individual squad members of the three squads of the Munich riot control unit were not interviewed. The applicants had requested that they be interviewed, as the evidence had suggested that the alleged perpetrators had belonged to one of these three squads. The investigating police unit was also provided with video surveillance recorded by the 23rd platoon of the 6th Dachau public-order support force battalion. It was established that the original video tapes and possible digital copies had already been deleted and that only the excerpts were still available. The Munich general public prosecutor confirmed the decision of the public prosecutor’s office of 4 August 2009 to discontinue the investigation. The applicants appealed and pointed out that the members of the deployed squads had still not been questioned and that the inspected videos were fragmentary, but nonetheless contradicted certain parts of the statements made by the squad leaders. On 19 September 2011 the Munich Court of Appeal declared the applicants’ application to force further enquiries inadmissible. On 25 October 2011 the applicants lodged a constitutional complaint, relying on Articles 2 § 2, 19 § 4 and 103 § 1 of the German Basic Law (G.C.P.C.) The Federal Constitutional Court refused, in a reasoned decision (2 BvR 1304/12), to admit the applicants’ constitutional complaint. The court held that the investigations had been conducted diligently, but had not established sufficient suspicion of criminal conduct on the part of specific police officers. A subsequent appeal before the Munich general public prosecutor was to no avail. The investigation against the five police officers was discontinued by the Munich public prosecutor’s office. The applicants alleged that several relevant parts of the video material, showing disproportionate police violence, had been deleted. They also filed criminal complaints in respect of assistance given in an official capacity in avoiding prosecution or punishment.

The case was assigned to the newly constituted Fifth Section (Rule 25§ 5 and Rule 52§ 1) The applicant was born in 1962 and lives in Izmir and was represented by Mr K. Bilgiç. He was charged with forging passport, in particular arranging for false visa stamps for travelling abroad. The Izmir State Security Court issued a decision of lack of jurisdiction ratione materiae and referred the case to the Court of Cassation for determination. On 25 March 1999 the Court Of Cassation overturned the Izmir Assize Court’s decision and held that the offence in question was within the latter's jurisdiction. The case-file was therefore sent to the IzMir Assize court and held eight hearings between 22 March 2001 and 3 December 2003. All hearings prior to the seventh one, which was held on 5 June 2003, were postponed on the ground that the address of one of the co‑accused, namely A.G., could not be found.

EUR 2,500) The court found that the 2004 Act produced legal effects as from the date of entry into force (17 September 2004) Its provisions applied retroactively to all proceedings in which delays had occurred before that date and had not yet been remedied. It acknowledged that there had been a delay at the initial stage of proceedings but found that this situation had ceased to exist when the2004 Act entered into force.

The applicant was taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation. He was charged with carrying out activities for the purpose of bringing about the secession of part of the national territory. In the course of the criminal proceedings, the Diyarbakır State Security Court held thirty hearings and heard seventeen witnesses. On 3 June 1999 the applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to death under Article 125 of the Criminal Code. Taking into account the applicant's conduct during the trial, the death penalty was commuted to a life sentence. On 21 February 2000 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the State security Court.

The applicant, Mr. Bengt Pudas, is a Swedish citizen born in 1959. He lives at Hedenäset, which is situated in the Municipality of Övertorneå and the County of Norrbotten, in the North of Sweden. The County Administrative Board granted him a taxi traffic licence, and, on 20 May, a licence to carry passengers and their goods on specified interurban routes (linjetrafik) The licences were expressed in writing. The Court heard addresses by Mr. Corell for the Government, by Mr Gaukur Jörundsson for the Commission and by Mr Ravnsborg for the applicant, as well as their replies to its questions. The applicant commenced his combined taxi and interurban traffic business on 20 May 1980. Two vehicles (a Peugeot 505 and Citroën) were used in the business, which occupied the applicant, his father and a third driver on a part-time basis. The applicant offered a service of two journeys a week at scheduled times. This service was available on request and had to be ordered one day in advance. The County Traffic Company at the same time requested that this licence be revoked, as well as a licence held since 1973 by a certain Mr. Wälimaa. In support of its application, the Company submitted that two traffic services in two different regions were to be united into one regular service with a single time-table. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Board of Transport (transportrådet), in which he alleged, inter alia, the following. The County Traffic Company’s application for a licence for the routes covered by his licence had been motivated not by any public interest in improving the transport service. Only very serious reasons, such as misconduct of the licence-holder, could justify revocation. When revoking his licence, the County Administrative Board had failed to take due account of his interests. The transport service on the routes concerned was not likely to be improved simply by being carried out by Mr. Wälimaa and others instead of by himself.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36590/97) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The respondent State was to pay the applicant FRF 10,000 (ten thousand French francs) in damages. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). On 6 April 2000 the application was declared partly admissible. The case was referred to the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights. The case was heard in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 6 March 2002. The Court heard addresses by the Government and the applicant's counsel, as well as their replies to questions from individual members of the Court. A separate opinion of Judges Makarczyk and Türmen was annexed to the judgment. The judge decided that the case should be sent back to the Court of General Jurisdiction for reconsideration. The decision was made to impose a fine on the Government of France of FRF 4,100 (four thousand one hundred French francs) received by way of legal aid to be converted into Turkish liras on 9 November 2000. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his right of access to court was breached by the domestic court’s refusal of his legal aid request. He claimed that he had become ill during his military service as a result of the degrading treatment he had been subjected to in the army. He requested a total of 150,000 Turkish liras (TRY) in both pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages, submitting the medical records from the Van Military Hospital in support of his claims. He also requested legal aid for the court fees, presenting a certificate from the headman (muhtar) attesting to his poverty. On 4 February 2009 the Supreme Military Administrative Court decided to discontinue the compensation proceedings because the applicant had not paid the necessary court fees. The applicant had to pay a total of TRY 2,384 (approximately EUR 1,300) in court fees within thirty days for the proceedings to be continued. The case was settled in favor of the applicant, who received a settlement of approximately $1.2 million (EUR 1.3 million) in compensation. The trial was adjourned until the end of February 2009. The compensation was settled out of court and the case was dismissed on February 18, 2009, after the applicant paid the court fees for the case.

He said: ‘When a body is charged by statute with the power or duty, which cannot be done, it cannot be allowed to be biased.’ Jowitt said that if, contrary to his finding, there was unconscious bias, the “doctrine of necessity” fell to be considered. He concluded that, on the evidence before him, he could not say that the applicant had established that there had been a real danger of injustice having occurred as a result of bias. The court is [not] concerned strictly with the appearance of bias but rather with establishing the possibility thatthere was actual although unconscious bias.

Jowitt J. said the court must reach its own factual conclusion on the facts. He concluded that there was no unconscious bias on the part of any of the Panel members. The court is not concerned strictly with the appearance of bias but rather with establishing the possibility thatthere was actual although unconscious bias, Jowitt said. He said: “When a body is charged by statute with the power or duty, which cannot be questioned, the court cannot reach a conclusion which is not based on the evidence.” The court’s conclusion ‘personifies the reasonable man’, he said, adding that ‘a real danger clearly involves more than a minimal risk, less than a probability’.

The court must reach its own factual conclusion on the facts. A real danger clearly involves more than a minimal risk, less than a probability. It is not necessary for the applicant to demonstrate a real possibility that the ... decision would have been different but for the bias. What must be established is the real danger of bias having affected the decision in the sense of having caused the decision-maker, albeit unconsciously, to weigh the competing contentions, and so decide the merits, unfairly. The court is [not] concerned strictly with the appearance of bias but rather with establishing the possibility that there was actual although unconscious bias.” Jowitt J. stated, further, that if, contrary to his finding, there was unconscious bias on the part of the Panel, the “doctrine of necessity” fell to be considered.

He had argued that the Board had failed to take the reasonable step of appointing an independent panel to hear evidence and report to the Panel. Jowtt J. rejected the submission, on the grounds that no useful reference could have been made to an independent tribunal which did not involve an impermissible delegation. The applicant failed to establish that the Panel’s decision was irrational or unreasonable or to make out any sufficient ground for judicial review.

The Court of Appeal refused an application for leave to appeal from Jowitt J.'s decision. The decision will not be liable to be impugned on account of bias provided that: (i) if only some of those charged with the power or duty to decide are potentially affected by bias such of them as can lawfully withdraw from the decision making do so; and (ii) those of the decision makers who are potentially influenced by bias use their best endeavours to avoid the effect of bias. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 24746/94) against the United Kingdom lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that his son Pearse Jordan had been unjustifiably shot and killed by a police officer and that there had been no effective investigation into, or redress for, his death. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force. The proceedings in the present case should be conducted simultaneously with those in the cases of McKerr v. the United. Kingdom, no. 28883/95, Kelly and Others v the. United Kingdom,No. 30054/96 and Shanaghan v the U.K. no. 37715/97 (see judgments of the same date).  Pearse Jordan, aged 22, was shot and killed in Belfast by an officer of the Royal Ulster Constabulary (the RUC), later identified as Sergeant A. Treacy. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court heard addresses by Mr Weatherup and Mr Treacy and declared the application admissible on 4 April 2000. The facts of the case, in particular concerning what happened when PearseJordan was shot on 25 November 1992, are in dispute between the parties. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal and the jury returned a verdict in favour of the applicant. Four men heard a crash and saw a police car ram a car. Pearse Jordan emerged from the immobilised car, and appeared shaken. He staggered across the road towards the four men followed by four police officers. An officer about 12 feet away fired a number of shots. The civilians heard no warning shout or challenge given by any of the officers. The police carried out a search of the car. An official RUC statement stated that a deputy superintendent of the RUC from outside Belfast would investigate the shooting. In a later statement, it was announced that the Independent Commission for Police Complaints (the ICPC) would supervise the R UC investigation. Sergeant A was carrying a Smith and Wesson 59 pistol and a MP5 Heckler and Koch. He had been at a briefing at 11 a.m. the day before concerning reports of a planned distribution of kit and munitions, including weapons, explosives and mortars, by the Provisional IRA in West Belfast. A surveillance operation was to be mounted and he was in charge of the teams on the ground which were going to intervene if possible to intercept the munitions. He was told by radio to gather his people together – car crews with call signs 8, 9, 3 and 12. When the red Orion left Arizona street, he and his crews left the police station but were called back almost immediately. Sergeant A saw the driver running across the road from left to right at an angle away from him. He could not see the man’s hands which were below his waist. He feared the man was armed as he had spun round so quickly. He fired a short burst from his MP5 at the trunk of the man. The driver fell flat, toppling over. It was realised at that stage that he was seriously injured. Sergeant A quickly searched the car, while other security force personnel administered first aid to the driver. He directed most of the police officers to leave the scene as soon as they had arrived, including crew 12 in their car. Sergeant A said that he had a clear view of the deceased from the waist up. When the deceased turned to face him, he did not make any movements towards him. In that short space of time, he formed the opinion that the deceased was a threat to his life. The man’s actions had not been of someone about to surrender. He was certain that there were no viable alternatives to discharging his own weapon. Forensic examinations of the cars involved in the incident were carried out. Interviews were conducted with the other police officers and army personnel involved. Only officer D heard shouting coming from the call sign 8 direction before the shooting. The RUC concluded its inquiry into the death of Pearse Jordan in May 1993. Its report on the investigation was submitted to the Director of Public Prosecutions (the DPP) On 16 November 1993, the DPP’s department issued to the Chief Constable of the RUC a direction of “no prosecution” in respect of the fatal shooting. Following that decision, the Coroner decided to hold an inquest. The Coroner wrote to interested parties informing them that the inquest would begin on 4 January 1995. The inquest concluded on 8 January 1995 with the verdict of unlawful killing. The applicant and his family were not provided with any indication as to the nature of the. RUC's findings. At the Coroner’s inquest on 4 January 1995, the applicant and his family were represented by a solicitor and counsel. The Coroner sat for three and a half days, hearing evidence from 19 witnesses, including the applicant, 8 civilians, Soldiers V, W and X, 7 police officers and a pathologist. Defence issued a certificate in which he identified information whose disclosure at the inquest he believed would be contrary to the public interest on grounds of national security. Defence made an application that the identities of certain military witnesses be withheld and that they should give their evidence from behind a screen. The DPP decided that the evidence remained insufficient to warrant the prosecution of any person in relation to Pearse Jordan's death. The applicant's legal representatives made an application for the Coroner to discharge himself from the Inquest on the grounds that he was not conducting the inquest fairly. The applicant sought orders of certiorari to quash inter alia (a) the. Coroner’s refusal to give the next of kin access to the statements of the witnesses. before they gave evidence at the inquest and (b) the decision of the Cor. to grant anonymity to RUC witnesses. By judgment of 11 December 1995, Lord Justice Carswell refused the applicant's claims. In doing so he had regard to the inquisitorial nature of inquest proceedings. The applicant appealed against the decision of Lord Justice Carswell. The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland. The applicant’s application for leave to appeal to the House of Lords was refused. The inquest was due to recommence on 1 December 1997. However, it was adjourned on 19 November 1997 by the Coroner, after consultation with the parties, pending the outcome of a judicial review application in the High Court concerning the availability of legal aid for legal representation for the family of the deceased at inquests. The Coroner informed the interested parties that he intended to resume the inquest on 1 November 1999. On 2 February 2000, the applicant was informed that the Chief Constable would provide copies of the statements of the witnesses to appear at the inquest. The applicant was granted legal aid to pursue a civil action for compensation in the High Court. On 5 October 1995, the applicant served a statement of claim in the civil proceedings. On 8 October 1999, the Crown Solicitor wrote to the applicant seeking consent to a remittal of the civil action to trial. The applicant stated that the case is currently at the discovery stage but that this cannot be concluded until the inquest is terminated. On 2 October 2000 the applicant was provided with the witness statements of persons whom the Coroner has decided should be called to give evidence at the inquest. in addition to the witnesses who gave evidence in January 1995, 12 police officers and Soldier Y.

In response to the enquiry made in accordance with the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him.

The Court heard evidence from representatives of the German Government and the German people in a hearing held on 24 January 1990. The documents were submitted on 9, 10 and 25 April 1990. They were required to be submitted on the 24th day of the hearing. The hearing was adjourned until the next day. The court ruled that the documents should be submitted in full. The case was heard for the first time on 23 April 1990 and the case was decided in favour of the Government. The Court decided that the case should be returned to the Government and not the Court of Appeal. The decision was appealed to the European Court of Human Rights for review.

The hearing was to take place on January 24, 1990, at the Court of Justice of Germany. The issue was whether there was a need to hold the hearing. It was decided that the hearing should take place that day. The case was heard for the first time on January 25, 1990. The court ruled that there was no need for the hearing to be held that day, as it had already been held earlier that day in the same court. The hearing was adjourned until January 26, when it was expected that the papers would be submitted again. The papers were finally submitted and the case was decided in favor of the request for a stay of the trial.

The Court heard the case for the first time on December 14, 1989. The issue was whether there was a need for a written order to be submitted to the Court. The Court decided that there was no need for such a request. The case was decided in favour of the application of Article 50 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) The case led to the creation of the ECHR, the European Court of Human Rights, and the European Commission of Justice. The ECHR ruled that the case should be heard by the Court of Justice, rather than by an international court of law. The hearing was adjourned until April 9, 1990. It was decided that the matter should be returned to the ECHR on April 18, 1990, and that it should not be heard again until after.

In 1974 a dispute arose between the applicant and the company concerning various paid activities which it proposed to withdraw from him. On 10 March 1978, the day following the first hearing, he was suspended from his duties by his employer. The company considered that it was entitled to take such a decision at any time without giving reasons. The first round of the proceedings concerning the applicant’s suspension was concluded in November 1981. On 23 April 1981 the Linz Labour Court dismissed the applicant's claims. The case was therefore remitted to the Labour Court. The court dismissed the remainder of the appeal, finding that, under Article 228 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a declaratory judgment may bear only on the existence of a legal relationship. On 21 May 1980 Mr Obermeier had been declared disabled for the purposes of the Disabled Persons (Employment) Act. On 8 May 1981, the company had sought the authorisation for the applicant’s dismissal. Following a hearing, the Board gave its consent to the dismissal on 8 July 1981, finding that the relationship of trust between the parties had been irremediably undermined. The Provincial Governor (Landeshauptmann) for Upper Austria confirmed the Board's decision on 16 October 1981. The applicant then appealed to the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof) which dismissed his appeal on 9 March 1983. The company pleaded Mr Obermeier’s lack of a legal interest (Rechtsschutzbedürfnis) in the revocation of his suspension, since in the meantime he had been dismissed. The applicant, for his part, challenged the lawfulness of his dismissal. He stressed in particular that it had been pronounced before the authorisation from the Disabled Persons Board had become final, as the case was still pending before the Administrative Court. The company sent to the applicant, on 21 December 1984, a further notification of dismissal, which was to take effect on 30 June 1985. On appeal by the company, the applicant appealed on points of law to the Supreme Court which quashed the decisions of the labour courts. Following the Supreme Court’s order of 23 October 1984 remitting the applicant's case to it, the Linz Labour Court allowed his claim on 30 January 1985. The applicant appealed on points of law to the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) which referred the case to the Administrative Court. The latter court allowed the appeal on 21 May 1986, finding that the company had committed an error of law by dismissing Mr Obermeier before the authorisation had become final. The Board and the Provincial Governor found, on 10 February 1986 and 12 January 1987 respectively, that they lacked jurisdiction to make such a declaration. The Supreme Court stated that it was not for the civil courts to review the decisions of the administrative authorities. Mr Obermeier also challenged his dismissal in the labour courts. On 23 June 1988 in a supplementary memorial he stressed that for his second dismissal no valid prior consent had been obtained from the works council as was required under clause 33 § 9 of the collective agreement. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 29 June, holding that section 105 of the Industrial Relations Act did not apply to a disabled person. The court dismissed the action on 23 September 1988, finding that the agreement given by the worksCouncil in 1981 was also valid in relation to the 1984 dismissal. The case dates back to December 1984, when Mr Obermeier was fired from his job. He appealed the dismissal of 21 December 1984 and the authorisation given by the administrative bodies to the company. The Supreme Court quashed these two decisions but dismissed his application on 14 March 1990, on the ground that the judicial decisions which had closed the proceedings in which the applicant had already contested the validity of his dismissal in the labour courts were final. The court took the view that the administrative organs in question had, by implication, expressed their opinion on the matter.

Saïd André Remli, a French national of Algerian origin, is currently in custody at Les Baumettes Prison in Marseilles. While attempting to escape from Lyons-Montluc Prison, the applicant and a fellow prisoner, Mr Boumédienne Merdji, knocked out a warder, who died four months later as a result of the blows he had received. The two prisoners were charged with intentional homicide for the purpose of facilitating, preparing or executing the offences of escape and attempted escape. In a judgment of 12 August 1988 the Indictment Division of the Lyons Court of Appeal committed them for trial at the Rhône Assize Court. On the first day, when the sitting began, the members of the jury and two additional jurors were drawn by lot.

The trial at the Assize Court took place on 12, 13 and 14 April 1989. The defendants challenged five jurors, the legal maximum, and the prosecution two. One of the jurors made the remark that she was a racist. The jury was subsequently empanelled and the hearing of witnesses began. Mr Remli is currently in custody at Les Baumettes Prison in Marseilles. The trial is expected to last until the end of May this year. The verdicts are expected to be delivered at the close of the trial on May 25th 1989. For more information on the trial see the Rhône Assize court’s website.

On 14 April 1989 the Assize Court sentenced Mr Remli to life imprisonment and Mr Merdji to a twenty-year term, for two-thirds of which he would not be liable to any form of release. He appealed on points of law. In a judgment of 22 November 1989 the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal. It gave the following reason in particular: “The Assize court rightly refused to take formal note of events which, assuming they were established, had taken place outside the hearing, such that it could not have been in a position to note them.’” The Court rejected the appeal on the grounds that the Court was not able to take a formal note.

It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant was born in 1969 and lives in İstanbul. He was severely wounded by gunshots during a clash between the security forces and a group of terrorists in 1990. In 1992 he was declared to be suffering from a permanent disability and discharged from the army. In 2004 a CT scan revealed an unidentified metallic object in the left orbital area. In 2007, the applicant was admitted to the neurosurgery department of the GATA Military Hospital and a scan revealed that he had a bullet in his head. The Supreme Military Administrative Court rejected both actions as being out of time. In both decisions the court held that notwithstanding the fact that the applicant had not been aware of the bullet in his head until 2007, pursuant to section 43(1) of the Supreme Military administrative court Act, his compensation claims should have been lodged within five years of the incident. Its decision was served on the applicant on 6 May 2009. The applicant was awarded compensation for the injuries he. sustained on account of a bullet which had been found in. his head in 2007. The court said that the injuries were not so serious that they should not have been considered as a cause for compensation.

The European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) provides for the right to contract and to be a party to such contracts. The ECHR also provides for a right to compensation for damage caused by the actions of one of the parties to a contract. The right to a compensation for any loss or damage caused as a result of a contract is also part of the EHR. The rights of parties to contract with each other are not subject to the ECHR's rules, except in certain limited circumstances, such as when they are for the benefit of the public, or when the parties are involved in a dispute over the rights of the other party.

Annex I of the ESA Convention states that all parties to the contract are entitled to the right to contract. Article 33 of the Convention also stipulates that the Board must rescind any decision that is contrary to the rules of the Agreement. The Board can also make such a decision without prejudice to the other party's right to compensation. The board has the power to make such decisions without prejudice, even if the decision is not in line with the rules. The Court of Appeal can also order the board to rescind a decision if it is in breach of the rules or the decision of the Court of Appeals. The decision to rescind the decision can be appealed to the European Court of Justice, which is in charge of the case. The court can also issue an order to remove a decision made by the Court.

The European Parliament is not required to make such a decision in the first place, but it must make it if there is a compelling reason to do so. If there is no compelling reason, then there is not a reason to make the decision. The only exception to this is that if the decision is to be made in the interests of national security.

The guarantees provided have been considered sufficient for the Court, the Audiencia Nacional ruled on 3 June 2015, dismissing the súplica appeals lodged by the applicant. Andres Lopez Elorza is charged with having been a member of a conspiracy to import heroin into the United States. He is seeking extradition to stand trial on federal narcotics offenses in the Eastern District of New York. He has appealed to the Constitutional Court to stay his extradition pending the outcome of proceedings before the Court. The application was rejected on 1 July 2015. On 23 July 2015 the Government submitted their response and attached a document issued by the Office of International Affairs of the US Department of Justice called “supplemental information to Spain on Sentencing Issues in Relation to Andres Lopez Flores’ (hereinafter, “the US report”) The charges followed the search, in January 2005, of a farm Lopez Elorza operated in Medellin, Colombia. The six puppies were bound for the United States, and the heroin they carried was surgically removed. A timely admission of guilt is a factor which could reduce the sentence the judge decides to impose following a conviction. The agreement may include, inter alia, an agreement to cooperate with U.S. authorities. The judge may also decline to approve an agreement she or he does not believe to be in the interests of justice, the government says. The plea agreement may also include the parties’ recommendation as to the appropriate sentence that may or may not bind the judge regarding the sentence that will be imposed. The US report stressed that the Guidelines were advisory since the judge had ‘the discretion to impose a sentence outside the applicable Guidelines range so long as the court states ‘with specificity,’ both at sentencing and in the written judgment and commitment order, its reason for doing so’ The decision whether to sentence a person convicted of multiple counts concurrently or consecutively was at the discretion of the court. The report also stressed the following: “Prior to sentencing, a probation officer will prepare a presentence report that contains information about the defendant’s offense, his criminal history, other background information, and a calculation of the advisory sentencing range” According to the US Federal Sentencing Guidelines, the advisory sentencing range was “188 to 235 months incarceration, far less than the possible life sentence provided for under the statutes with which he was charged” The report stated that under section 3553(a) of Title 18 of the US Code, there was a “need to avoid unwarranted sentence disparities”. Several of the applicant’s co-conspirators had already been sentenced in a related case before the same judge who had been assigned to the applicant's case. One of the co- conspirators “faced a Guidelines range of 188 to 235 years and received a sentence of 72 months incarceration”, the report stated. The report concluded that while it was possible that any available maximum sentence could be imposed for an offence, under the circumstances present in this case, “the risk of López Elorza receiving such a sentence is low”. The sentences imposed on the applicant’s co-conspirators by the same judge “[could] be of value in assessing the sentence that will be imposed on him” and a third had “faced a Guidelines range of 70 to 87 months and received a sentence of Time Served (approximately 12 months incarceration)” The US report also noted that none of those defendants had entered into cooperation agreements with the government. The applicant could also seek executive clemency in the form of commutation (reduction) of his sentence. In cases similar to the applicant’s, commutation of life sentences was not ‘a rare occurrence’. The report noted that of 13 July 2015, when President Obama had commuted the life sentences of “fourteen persons who had been convicted of drug related offenses”. On 31 July 2015 the interim measures under Rule 39 were extended and the Court requested that the Government stay the applicant's extradition to the United States while the proceedings were pending before the Court. It gave as an example that of 14 persons who were convicted of ‘drug-related offenses’ in July 2015.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 48539/99) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained of the use of covert audio and video surveillance within his cell, the prison visiting area and upon a fellow prisoner. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The parties responded to the observations in writing. The case was heard by the Chamber of the European Court of Justice. The application was made after David Beesley was murdered. The applicant and Leroy Grant were held for long periods in the same cell and recordings of their conversations were made from 20 February to 12 March 1995. A police informant with a criminal record was placed in the applicant's cell for the purpose of eliciting information from the applicant. Telephone conversations between H. and the police included comments by the police instructing H. to “push him for what you can” and disclosed evidence of concerted police coaching. After 20 April 1995 he associated regularly with the applicant who was remanded at Strangeways Prison. On 28 June 1995 the applicant was taken away from the prison to be interviewed by thePolice concerning the Kwik-Save robbery. The applicant was interviewed again in the presence of his solicitor on 29 June and 26 July 1995 and remained silent when faced with the allegations. The thrust of the applicant's case was that he was discussing robberies and did not accede to H.'s efforts to channel their conversation into a discussion of the murder. No evidence, other than the alleged admissions, connected the applicant with the killing of Mr Beesley. The judge concluded that there was evidence on the tapes from which the jury could infer that the applicant was involved in the events of 3 February 1995, and it was not so unreliable that it could not be left to the jury to assess for themselves. The judge's ruling on the admissibility of the evidence was given on 26 January 1998, after a voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of a jury) and consisted of a judgment of eighteen pages. H. was accordingly admitted before the jury. In his summing-up to the jury on 10 and 11 February 1998, the trial judge gave directions on the way in which the jury should assess the reliability of the disputed evidence. He told them that they were to judge whether the police had deliberately wound up the applicant during the interview on 28 June 1995 and how to approach the evidence put forward by H. The applicant was convicted of murder in 1998 and sentenced to life imprisonment. He appealed against his conviction, but was refused leave to appeal by a single judge. His renewed application was refused by the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) on 18 January 1999, after a hearing at which he was represented by leading counsel. In the court's judgment of that date, Lord Justice Rose found that the trial judge gave a very careful and impeccable ruling as regards the admissibility of the tapes and evidence put forward by H.S. and H.N. He also argued that the judge had erred in his directions as to the circumstances in which the jury could draw inferences from the applicant's failure to respond to police questions.

The Albanian Government did not inform the Court of their wish to intervene in the proceedings. The hearing before the Barcelona Audiencia Provincial took place on 19 April 2006. N. attended the hearing after undergoing a psychological diagnosis which established her suitability to testify in court. She had started to answer the questions posed by the public prosecutor when her statement had to be interrupted. She was said to be suffering from post‑traumatic stress symptoms that were hindering her from testifying. Those symptoms were medically confirmed after the hearing. The court had already adjourned the hearing once before, following a similar reaction on the part of N. As a consequence, it had provided her with psychological assistance before and during the hearing to allow for her full examination, but to no avail. The court had previously attempted – perhaps to the point of excess – to exhaust all remedies to obtain her statement. The witness rightly started her statement by giving a detailed description of the evolution of her relationship with the accused. Her determination began to weaken when, with slightly shaking hands, she began to describe the assaults she had suffered on the second day. The shaking later developed into an uncontrollable trembling of her mouth and her entire body. Whether she was encouraged to stand up, sit down, drink water or have her hands held, nothing was of the slightest help to calm her down. Only continuous breaks and recesses and an excessive effort on her part enabled her to make, in more that an hour, some progress. Her testimony essentially corroborated her pre-trial statement and proved the authenticity of her post-traumatic stress. Barcelona Audiencia Provincial ordered that the statements which had been taken from her during the investigation stage of the proceedings be read out. The applicant gave his alternative account of the facts. The court found that on 4 April 2004 the applicant had gone to N.’s apartment and had made death threats when she had not let him in to see their son. Upon leaving the apartment, he had twice knocked a car belonging to J., a close male friend of N., causing damage to the vehicle. On 6 April 2004 at around 1 a.m., the. applicant had broken in through a window. He had punched J., who had been there with N., and then hit N. repeatedly. It also found that after those three hours had elapsed, the applicant. had abducted N. into his car after having ordered J. to take the child to an address which he would provide later by telephone. The applicant was sentenced as the principal offender for: (i) making very serious threats to N., to fifteen months’ imprisonment; (ii) breaking and entering into N.’s home using violence and coercion, to two and a half years’. imprisonment. (iii) causing minor bodily injuries to J., to twelve days’ house arrest; (iv) N.'s kidnapping under threat, with the aggravating factor of family ties, to eight years' imprisonment. He was also fined EUR 30,525 for damages. The court found that, when the applicant had been arrested at Prat de Llobregat Airport (Barcelona), he had been carrying false identification documents. The Supreme Court quashed the Audiencia Provincial’s judgment. The court considered that the use as evidence of the victim's pre-trial statements had not infringed the applicant's right to defend himself. The judge also considered the reliability of N.’ s statement had been enhanced when confronted with the applicant’S implausible statement. The Supreme Court reduced the penalty imposed on the applicant in respect of kidnapping. It also lessened the classification of the offence of making threats. It acquitted the applicant of the crime against moral integrity because, in the instant case, this crime could be considered to come under the offences of rape. Supreme Court said trial courts should take special care in assessing victims’ statements when they are the sole direct evidence against the accused. The law permitted that pre-trial statements could be read out in the courtroom as an alternative when a witness’s testimony could not be produced owing to circumstances beyond the parties’ control. The Supreme Court added that the delay with which N. had reported the facts to the police could be explained by her fear and by the fact that she had had a child with the applicant. The applicant lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court. In a decision served on 3 July 2008, the appeal was declared inadmissible for being devoid of any constitutional content.

The property was covered by an area plan (områdesplan - see paragraph 26 below), adopted in 1972, which described the property mainly as a public area containing green spaces, streets and car parking. This prohibition has subsequently been prolonged by the Board for one or two years each time, leaving the property unaffected for only a few brief intermediate periods. The last decision was taken on 11 July 1985 and was valid until 11 July 1987. On 1 July 1987, with the entry into force of the Plan and Building Act 1987, the existing system for prohibitions on construction was abolished and replaced by a new one. Municipal Assembly (kommunfullmäktige) adopted a master plan (generalplan) relating to part of the municipality of Botkyrka, according to which the applicant’s property was supposed to be used for building blocks of flats of more than two storeys. The Building Committee stated, in reply to a request from the applicant, that it was not prepared to grant him an exemption from the building prohibition or a permit to build a one-family house and a garage on the property. The Board rejected the appeal on 25 April 1980. In April 1983 the Building Committee requested the Board to revoke, pursuant to section 168 of the 1947 Act, the right to build according to the subdivision plan of 1938. The applicant appealed to the Government, which rejected the appeal on 15 December 1983. The Building Committee conceded that a mistake had been made and quashed its decision of 12 June. The applicant appealed against the Board’s decision to the Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten) of Stockholm. On 24 April 1986 the Government quashed the Board's decision, holding that the Committee's opinion was not a binding decision and that, accordingly, it could not as such be subject to an appeal. The application to the Supreme Court for leave to appeal was rejected on 1 November 1988. The case is still pending in the High Court of Sweden. The applicant again filed a request for a preliminary opinion regarding a building permit for his property. The Building Committee decided however, pursuant to the rules laid down in the new 1987 Act, to defer its decision for a period of two years. The validity of the subdivision plan (see paragraph 8 above) remained unaffected. The application was rejected on the grounds that it was too small to be considered as a site for building a town plan. The applicant appealed the decision, and the decision was eventually overturned by the Court of Appeal. The case was heard for the first time on 6 July 1987. The hearing was adjourned until 9 July 1987, when the applicant's application was approved.

The applicant was born in 1973 and lives in Les Salles Sur Verdon, France. At the beginning of the 1990s a new concept called “tax asset stripping cases’ (selskabstømmersager) came into existence in Denmark. The persons involved committed aggravated debtor fraud by buying up and selling numerous inactive, solvent private limited companies. They then “stripped” the companies of assets, including deposits earmarked for corporation tax. According to surveys made by the customs and tax authorities, approximately one thousand six hundred companies with a total tax debt exceeding two billion Danish kroner (DKK) were stripped in the period from the late 1980s until 1994.

The applicant was born in 1973 and lives in Les Salles Sur Verdon, France. On 19 September 1995 the applicant was arrested and charged, inter alia, with aggravated debtor fraud. On the same day he was detained in solitary confinement, which was prolonged at regular intervals until he was released on 22 December 1995. From January 1996 to June 1998 various investigative steps were taken, notably relating to five co-accused in the case, for example searches in Denmark, Switzerland and Sweden.

eval_texts: Cases originated in two application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The first applicant alleged that his trial for indecent assault had been unfair because one of the two women who made complaints against him died before the trial and her statement to the police was read to the jury. The second applicant alleged. that his. trial for wounding with intent to do grievous bodily harm had been. unfair because the statement of one witness who feared attending trial was read. to the Jury. The applicants and the Government each filed written observations. A hearing in both cases took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 January 2008. The applicant was working as a consultant physician in the field of rehabilitative medicine. He was charged on two counts of indecent assault on two female patients while they were allegedly under hypnosis. One of the complainants, S.T., committed suicide before the trial but made a statement to the police. A preliminary hearing was held to determine whether the statement should be read to the jury. The judge allowed the evidence to be admitted at trial. The jury heard evidence from a number of different witnesses and the defence were given the opportunity to cross-examine other witnesses. In his summing up, the trial judge directed the members of the jury, on two separate occasions, as to how they should regard the read statement of the deceased complainant. The applicant was convicted by a unanimous verdict on both counts of indecent assault. On three occasions the jury asked for clarification of points raised in the read statement of S.T. account when considering her evidence. The Court of Appeal concluded on 3 November 2005 that the applicant's right to a fair trial had not been infringed. Relying on Doorson v the Netherlands, judgment of 26 March 1996, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1996‑II p 66, the court held that admissibility of evidence is primarily a matter of domestic law. It then found: “Where a witness who is the sole witness of a crime has made a statement to be used in its prosecution and has since died, there may be a strong public interest in the admission of the statement in evidence so that the prosecution may proceed” The Court of Appeal refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords but certified that a point of law of general public importance was involved in the decision. The court also considered that the applicant had been able to attack the accuracy of the deceased complainant's statement by exploring the inconsistencies between it and the evidence given by witnesses and experts. The applicant was charged with wounding with intent and also with attempting to pervert the course of justice by telling the police that he had seen two black men stab S. When witnesses were questioned at the scene, no-one claimed to have seen the applicant stab S., but two days later one of the witnesses, T., made a statement to police. T. was too fearful to attend trial before the jury. The trial judge heard evidence from a police officer who testified that the Iranian community was close-knit and that T.'s fear was genuine. T. himself gave evidence to the judge from behind a screen. In ruling that leave should be given for the statement to be read to the jury, the trial judge stated: “I am satisfied in those circumstances upon the criminal standard of proof that this witness is genuinely in fear” T. was found guilty under section 116(2) (e) and (4) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 (the “CJA 2003”). T.'s witness statement was then read to the jury in his absence. The applicant also gave evidence. On 29 April 2005, the applicant was convicted by a majority verdict, principally of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm. He was later sentenced to nine years' imprisonment to be served concurrently with a term of fifteen months' imprisonment for doing an act intended to pervert the course of justice. The Court of Appeal acknowledged, however, that the Crown accepted that T.'s statement was “both important and probative of a major issue in the case...and had it not been admitted the prospect of a conviction would have receded and that of an acquittal advanced” Appeal court ruled that the jury was properly informed of all matters necessary to its decision-making process. The applicant's sentence was reduced to seven years' imprisonment. Leave to appeal on conviction was refused on 24 January 2006. First instance said the trial judge had explicitly warned the jury in detail as to how they should treat this evidence and properly directed them to consider it in reaching their verdict. Second instance said that the judge had properly directed the jury and that even a proper direction by the judge could not cure the unfairness of the jury's verdict. Third instance stated that there was available not only cross-examination of other prosecution witnesses but also evidence from the applicant himself.

eval_texts: The case was brought before the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) by a group of Turkish citizens. The group wanted to claim compensation for work done in the U.S. during the 1990s. The ECHR ruled in favour of the group, and sent the case back to the ECHR. The case was returned to the ECHR, and the case will now be heard again. The application was made on August 24, 2013, and will be heard on September 14, 2013. The hearing is expected to last at least three days, with a decision expected by the end of the second week in September. The ECHR will then decide whether or not to grant the application for compensation. Workers claimed they had worked beyond the legal working time for the previous five years of their employment. Their work schedule did not take account of weekends or public holidays as the duty‑free shops remained open twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week. The İzmir Labour Court decided to join each applicant’s proceedings and to seek an expert report concerning the calculation of their claims for overtime, weekend and public holiday pay and remuneration for unused annual leave. On 14 July 2004 the expert submitted a report in which he noted that clause 25 (c) of the collective agreement concluded between the parties provided for an entitlement to overtime pay, calculated on the basis of one and a half times the hourly rate. Employer had previously been cautioned, on 25 November 1996, by the Ministry of Labour concerning its practices on working hours. Expert determined that the employer did not owe anything to the applicants for weekend and public holiday work as remuneration for those days had been in accordance with the applicable regulations. Expert also noted that the applicants could not claim any compensation for unused annual leave as they were still working at the company and such leave was only payable at the end of a contract. The applicants raised no objections to the expert’s conclusion on the dismissal of their claims for pay for work at the weekend and on public holidays and for unused. annual leave. Both parties appealed to the Court of Cassation. In September 2005 the İzmir Labour Court found in favour of the applicants in part and awarded them the amounts given in the expert’s report in respect of the unpaid overtime. It rejected their claims for pay for weekend and public holiday work and for unused annual leave. On 17 April 2006 the Court Of Cassation quashed the decision and remitted the case. In the resumed proceedings, the �ürzmir labour court requested that the expert amend the report. On 26 May 2008 the applicants were awarded the applicants compensation for overtime as determined in the revised expert report. However, as determined by the well-established case-law of the Grand Chamber of Grand Chamber the case was quashed on 28 October 2008. The applicants appealed against the decision and maintained that the fact that they had worked continuously for twenty-four hours had already been confirmed. Although they had proven that fact, the judgment had been based on the presumption that working for more than 14 hours a day was physically impossible. The Court of Cassation upheld the İzmir Labour Court’s decision without responding to the applicants’ objections. The applicants were awarded almost ninety percent less than the previous expert report had calculated. The decision was made by the Labour Court of the Turkish city of   Aydin. The application was dismissed on December 28, 2009, and the appeal was upheld on March 18, 2010.
