eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 8658/79) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission on 18 June 1979. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby Austria recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. The Government of the Federal Republic of Germany advised the Registrar, on 30 July 1984, that her Government did not intend to participate in the proceedings. The applicant, on the other hand, stated that he wished to participate and designated the lawyer who would represent him. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. F. Matscher, the elected judge of Austrian nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr. G. Wiarda. President Wiarda asked the Government to suspend the execution of fines imposed on Mr. Bönisch. Mr. Evrigenis and Mr. García de Enterría, who were prevented from taking part in the consideration of the case, were replaced by Mr. J. Cremona and Mr R. Bernhardt, substitute judges. On 17 January 1985, the Commission transmitted to the Registrar a number of documents whose production the Registrar had requested on the instructions of the President. On the same date, after consulting, through the Registrar, the Agent of the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicant, the President directed that the oral proceedings should open on 21 January (Rule 38) Hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The applicant, who is a citizen of the Federal Republic of Germany born in 1936, lives in Vienna. He runs a firm that specialises in meat smoking. The maximum quantity permissible in smoked meats of a carcinogenic substance called benzopyrene 3.4 was stated to be one part per (American) billion (“ppb’) The Court heard addresses and replies to its questions from Mr Türk, Mrs. Kabelka and Mr Lindner for the Government, Mr. Schermers for the Commission and Mr. Roessler for the applicant. In October 1976, the Market Office of the City of Vienna drew two samples of smoked meat from the production of the Bönisch company. The Institute was entrusted with carrying out the analysis of these samples. In its analysis, the Institute found a benzopyrene concentration of 2.7 and 3.0 ppb respectively and an excessive water content. The samples were therefore described as being dangerous to health and adulterated. This opinion by the Institute, which had been drafted on 28 November 1976, amounted to the lodging of a complaint. The case came before the same judge of the Regional Court who in 1976 had dealt with an earlier case against the applicant. The judge asked for the hearing of several experts. The expert explained in detail the method of analysis applied by his Institute. He emphasised that the products made by Mr. Bönisch’s firm showed a water content of 3.6 per cent, whereas, according to the Food Code (Codex Alimentarius Austriacus), it should not have exceeded 1.8 per cent. In a judgment delivered the same day (29 June 1978), the Regional Court found the applicant guilty of offences under section 56(1), nos. 1 and 2, and section 63(1) of the German food code. Mr. Bönisch appealed. He took issue with the Director of the Institute for not having adhered to the opinion of his colleagues. He also raised objections of principle against the appointment as court expert of the very person who had reported the case to the prosecuting authorities. The Vienna Court of Appeal rejected the appeal on 19 December 1978. The Regional Court had extensively dealt with all relevant aspects of the case before holding that the products made by the applicant were adulterated and dangerous to health. The carcinogenic effects of this substance were found to have been established by the Medical Faculty. The findings of the Regional Court were not open to doubt as they were based on the detailed detailed evidence. The Institute once more found an excessive concentration of benzopyrene (6.1 ppb) and an undeclared high water-content. Criminal proceedings were accordingly instituted against the applicant before the Vienna Regional Court. The case came before the same judge who again appointed the Director of the Institute as expert pursuant to section 48 of the 1975 Act. On the same day (20 September 1979), the Regional Court found the applicant guilty of offences against sections 56 and 63 of the Convention. The Court of Appeal ruled out the hearing of a counter-expert since the expert opinion obtained in the first-instance proceedings was not tainted with any defects (Articles 125 and 126 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) Mr. Bönisch appealed from this decision on grounds similar to those pleaded in the first proceedings (see paragraph 14 above) The Vienna Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on 20 May 1980. On 28 February 1984, the Federal President, exercising his power to grant a pardon, commuted the two prison sentences imposed on the applicant to fines of 30,000 and 15,000 Schillings (see paragraphs 13 and 17 above). The 1975 Act must be applied to all foodstuffs sold in Germany. The Act requires that the official who analysed the samples taken or drawn up the report should be appointed as expert. This expert must possess special professional qualifications and have a special authorisation from the Federal Ministry of Health (sections 47 and 50) The report (Anzeigegutachten) is sent to the Market Office, which in such cases transmits it to the public prosecutor’s department. The prosecuting authorities have to decide whether or not criminal proceedings should be brought, but they usually adhere to the Institute's opinion. Under Article 120 of the said Code, the prosecuting authorities and the accused are to be informed of the names of the experts appointed by the court. If any doubts persist or if the findings of these experts “are unclear, vague, contradictory“, the court may call another expert. Under the terms of Article 149 of the same Code, only the prosecutor and the defence counsel are entitled to put questions to witnesses and experts. Witnesses, on the contrary, do not have this possibility. The matter was debated in Parliament prior to the passing of the Act and subsequently in 1978 when a proposed amendment to section 48 was examined. This amendment, which was not in fact adopted, provided that both the Institute’s expert and any private expert called by the accused were to be heard only as witnesses. The receipt by Institute officials of certain bonus payments also gave rise to some discussion which subsequently provoked their discontinuance. Mr. Bönisch alleged, inter alia, that the proceedings taken against him had violated two provisions of Article 6: paragraph 1, in that they had not provided a fair trial, and paragraph 3 (d) (art. 6-3-d) in the first proceedings.

On 17 March 2008 the President of the Chamber to which the case had been allocated decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) The case was decided in favour of the applicant and he is currently detained at HMP Maghaberry, Northern Ireland. The applicant was arraigned on 8 June 2001 and pleaded not guilty to one count of possession of firearms and ammunition with intent. A defence statement was served on his behalf on 12 June 2001. He claimed that he may have been entrapped by a person known to him working with the police either for the purpose of incriminating him or his co-defendant. The applicant opposed the ex parte hearing of the prosecution's application by the disclosure judge. In non-jury trials in Northern Ireland, such an application is made to a judge other than the trial judge. That judge is designated by the Lord Chief Justice of Northern Ireland and is referred to as the ‘disclosure judge’ On 18 February 2002, the disclosure judge allowed the prosecution's application for non-disclosure. He outlined this Court's judgments in Rowe and Davis v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 28901/95, §§6 60-62, ECHR 2000‑II. The majority took the view that it was important for the trial judge to see the material personally. That is certainly true if the material is not prejudicial to the accused and where the trial is before a judge and jury. However, in the case [of] a non-jury trial it is obviously undesirable that prejudicial material which is not going to be part of the evidence should be seen by the judge. Especially if it is not disclosed to the defence. The judge decided that none of the material was likely to undermine the case for the prosecution or to assist the accused's defence. The judge then suggested that one way of proceeding would be to appoint special counsel who would be shown the material and remain throughout the trial. The trial judge then indicated that he had not received the disclosure judge's ruling or the statement of reasons and did not intend to receive anything that had not been made available to the defence. A hearing took place on 1 August 2002 to allow the parties and counsel appearing for the Attorney-General made submissions as to whether it was appropriate either for special counsel to be appointed or for the trial judge himself to consider the undisclosed material. The trial judge said that he considered that it was in the interests of justice that he should see the statement of reasons. He stressed that he had not himself seen the material seen by the disclosure judge. Counsel for the applicant's co-accused also suggested that the trial judge recuse himself since he had seen the statements of reasons which had not been made available to the defence. The trial judge ruled that he did not feel it was appropriate for him to recusing himself. The matter came before the disclosureJudge on 13 September 2002. In an ex tempore judgment he ruled: “There is no further safeguard that I am aware of that would be of any assistance, that one could conceive would be any assistance at this stage” The judge said there were two types of material involved in the case. The first could not assist the applicant because it was adverse to him. The second related to police procedures, was general in nature and content, and did not relate directly to the applicant. I would not regard the case as requiring the appointment of special counsel. I cannot foresee any circumstance in which the undisclosed material, that is the material undisclosed to the trial judge, would be of assistance to the defence. But it may be that the defence may advance a proposition or raise an issue that might by remote possibility make that so, and I think if the Crown concedes that that's the position then the Crown should make the matter known. ECHR 2003‑VII. Court of Appeal found that the applicant's defence of entrapment was well known to the trial judge, the prosecution, and the disclosure judge. eval_texts: Five Norwegian nationals lodged five applications against the Kingdom of Norway under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants complained that they did not have a fair and impartial hearing before the Borgarting High Court, whose judgment of 24 March 2003 was upheld by the Supreme Court on 25 September 2003. The applicants were members of a motor cycle club named “Screwdrivers”, which was based in Hamar and was, at the time of the events giving rise to the proceedings described below, the ‘Hang-Around Club’ of the Hells Angels. Drammen City Court acquitted the first, second and third applicants of counts I and II but convicted them of count III. Borgarting High Court rejected an appeal by the fourth applicant against a decision of 10 June 2002 by the City Court to prolong his provisional detention. The two co-defendants, B. and M., were convicted of all the charges and were sentenced respectively to 10 and 5 years' imprisonment. The fifth applicant was acquitted of all of the charges. The case is still ongoing and the defendants are still in provisional detention pending a final judgment. The trial is expected to last until the end of July 2002. The City Court had ordered detention of [the fourth applicant] on the ground of danger of evasion, see Article 171 (1) no. 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court found it correct to assess whether there were grounds for imprisonment on the basis of law enforcement considerations pursuant to Article 172. The basic condition stated in Article 172 is regarded as having been met. The defence counsel has alleged that the conviction is based on a statement of a co-defendant which is contradicted by other statements and evidence. This, and his personal circumstances as described by the defence counsel, are factors which indicate that thedanger of evasion is not sufficiently great. The High Court has found that the law enforcement considerations which form the basis of Article 172 are so prominent here that the accused should remain in prison also after judgment. The accused's personal and family circumstances pointed out by the defence counsel cannot be given sufficient weight in the opposite direction. Continued imprisonment cannot be said to be a disproportionate measure under Article 170A. Unless it is of importance for the decision regarding whether or not the accused is to be released, especially in relation to the consideration of proportionality, the regime he is now subject to is found to be of no importance to the High Court's assessment.” The High Court found that this rivalry in Nordic countries has led to a number of violent confrontations, including several deaths. The prosecution appealed against the acquittals of the first, second and third applicants on count II. The High Court was sitting with a jury of 11 members (reduced to 10 on the fifth day as one of the jury members was disqualified, see below) and with 3 professional judges. In the questions put to the jury the offences were described in the way set out in the indictment. The jury answered all the questions in the affirmative, except for one regarding count II with respect to the fourth applicant. The professional judges decided to pass judgment on the basis of thejury's verdict and, by a judgment of 24 March 2003, convicted all five applicants on counts I and III. For each applicant, the number of days spent in provisional detention was to be deducted from the sentence. The issue of compensation for pecuniary damage was postponed. Defence claimed decision of 1 July 2002 had implications for the other defendants. Member of jury claimed she had made a witness statement to the police that related to the case but her name had not been included on the list of witnesses. The Supreme Court unanimously rejected both appeal grounds, on procedure and sentencing, subject to certain adjustments to the number of days to be deducted on account of provisional detention. The first voting judge, Mr Justice Støle, gave inter alia the following reasons: “(13) I will first deal with the allegation that High Court judge, Judge G., was disqualified. ... (14) I find reason to point out that our rules of procedure for criminal cases in a High Court that sits with a jury are based on a distribution of functions.” The question of imprisonment was decided during the investigation and without a conviction by any court. The objection on the grounds of disqualification is not aimed at the presiding judge of the High Court, but at one of the other two professional judges who took part in the case. The question now is whether the other professional judges in a High Court that is convened with a jury are to be regarded as disqualified under section 108 of the Administration of Courts Act due to the fact that they have previously been involved in applying Article 172 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as a basis for imprisoning one or more of the accused in the same criminal case. I find that there are insufficient grounds for regarding the otherprofessional judges as being disqualified in such a situation. Judge G. of the High Court was not disqualified. It is true that all the professional judges take part in the assessment of whether the jury's decision is to form the basis of the judgment, or in exceptional cases be set aside. Such a setting aside of decisions does not determine the question of guilt and is also so exceptional that, in my opinion, it cannot be given any significance worth mentioning in this context. The jury was constituted with 11 members, according to Article 355 (2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Juror W. contacted a policeman she knew and asked if she could sit on the jury even though she had been questioned by the police on one occasion. The jury member reported to the police as a witness and told the police about her observations in close connection to the day of the explosion. Her observations are of such a nature that it can be questioned whether she is impartial in this case. After this, W. withdrew from the jury and the hearing continued with the remaining 10 jury members. The question here is whether W.'s presence as a member of the jury during the first four days of the hearing may have influenced the jury's verdict. I agree with the High Court that W. was prejudiced. But the question is then whether the other 10 members of the Jury became prejudiced as a result of W. serving on the jury. Jury member W. was at no time called as a witness in the case, by either the prosecuting authority or the defendants. The prosecutor has stated to the Supreme Court that the observations she had told to the police on 10 July 1997 – including about parts of the vehicle in question's licence number – were clarified early on as being of no importance to the further investigation. The jury foreperson has explained that the situation that arose after W. had withdrawn was discussed by the jury members and that they agreed that her participation during the first few days had not had any effect on the jury's verdict. (37) Accordingly, I cannot see that W.'s presence as a member of the jury can be regarded as a procedural error to which Article 343 (1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies.

The applicant alleged, inter alia, that she would be subjected to a real risk of ill-treatment and death by stoning if expelled from Turkey. She invoked Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention in respect of these two complaints. By a decision of 28 October 1999, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber having decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine), the parties replied in writing to each other.

The applicant met a man in Iran while attending a secretarial college. She fell in love with him and after some time they decided to get married. However, X’s family was opposed to their marriage. In June 1997 X married another woman. The applicant continued to see him and to have sexual relations with him. In November 1997 the applicant entered Turkey illegally. In February 1998 the applicant went to Istanbul, from where she tried to fly to Canada via France using a forged Canadian passport. When the applicant arrived at the airport in Paris, the French police found her to be in possession of a forged passport. She was held in detention at the Aliens Department until 26 March 1998. Thereafter, following the intervention of the Ankara branch office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), she was accommodated at a hotel in Istanbul.

In November 1997 the applicant entered Turkey illegally. In February 1998 the applicant went to Istanbul, from where she tried to fly to Canada via France using a forged Canadian passport. She was brought before the Bakırköy public prosecutor on the ground that she had entered Turkey with a forged passport in contravention of the Passport Act 1950. The public prosecutor ordered her release, finding she had not entered Turkey of her free will. The applicant was handed over to the Istanbul Security Directorate with a view to her deportation. When the applicant realised that she was going to be sent to Iran she told the Aliens Department she was an Iranian national.

The applicants are of Roma descent and lived in the village of Kosovo Polje. Following the outbreak of war in 1999, the first applicant refused to participate in the fighting and hid from the armed forces. Finally, they were driven out of their home by Albanian militia. They fled by train to Suvi Do, another village in Kosovo. They hid at a friend’s home, where they remained completely isolated from the world until they travelled to Sweden in 2006. They applied for asylum and permanent residence permits on arrival. On 13 March 2008 the Migration Board (Migrationsverket) rejected their applications. The applicants were not to be considered as refugees or as in need of any other specific protection.

His wife, who had been informed of the arrest on 16 February, spoke on the telephone to the Pfäffikon district prosecutor on 20 and 24 February. She asked him whether her husband had a lawyer. He replied that he had not but added that he would take care of it. In the second letter, which reached him on 28 February, she expressed the hope that the ‘lawyer’ - whose name she did not mention - “would look after [him]’  district prosecutor and return the other one to me (duly signed) It is my duty to point out to you that you are entitled to refuse to make any statement. Anything you say may be used in evidence against you. If you choose to remain silent, the district prosecutor will have to prove your guilt by other means (witnesses, etc.) He will usually then try to influence you by arguing that in that case you will remain in custody on remand until such time as he has questioned witnesses, other suspects, etc. If this does not worry you (i.e. a possible prolongation of your detention on remands), it will be to your advantage to exercise your right not to make a statement. Once I have received your authority to act, I shall apply for permission to visit you and will come and see you. At all events, be patient: you will haveto be released at some stage! Yours faithfully ...“ Mr. Durmaz was freed on 23 March 1984. The Zürich district prosecutor ordered that he had no case to answer as it could not be excluded beyond all possible doubt that someone else had been mistaken for him. It originated in an application (no. 15573/89) against Sweden lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Swedish national, Mr Torgny Gustafsson, on 1 July 1989. The object of the request and of the Government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed breaches by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6, 11 and 13 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 31).

The applicant owned the summer restaurant Ihrebaden at Ihreviken, Tingstäde, on the island of Gotland. The applicant also owned - and continues to own - the youth hostel Lummelunda at Nyhamn, Visby. The restaurant’s employees numbered less than ten. They were engaged on a seasonal basis, but had the option of being re-employed the following year. As the applicant was not a member of either of the two associations of restaurant employers, he was not bound by any collective labour agreement. It was, however, open to the applicant to accede to a collective agreement by accepting a substitute agreement.

The applicant and HRF rejected a substitute agreement on 16 July 1987. It would have required the employer to subscribe to five different insurance schemes on his employees' behalf. The employers' association and HRF agreed to a substitute agreement on 1 July 1987. The agreement was to replace a collective agreement between Ihrebaden and the Lummelunda youth hostel. The parties agreed that the most recent agreement would apply from 1 July to 31 December 1988. The employers’ association andHRF also agreed to subscribe to five insurance schemes on the employees’ behalf. The employment certificates would be issued on a ‘special form’. The employer would have to pay part of the ‘membership fees’ of the employees who had joined the HRF to cover the deducted part of their salary.

name: Samuel Betteridge
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he did not have a speedy review of the lawfulness of his detention. The application was communicated to the Government on 14 December 2010. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The case was decided to be heard by the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The decision to uphold the application was taken on 14 January 2011. The judge, Mr Justice Stephenson, ruled that the application could be heard. The Government was not entitled to appeal the decision.

The case originated in an application (no. 1497/10) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he did not have a speedy review of the lawfulness of his detention, in violation of Article 5. The application was communicated to the Government on 14 December 2010. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The case was decided to be heard by the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom and Northern Ireland on 25 January 2013. The Court ruled that the application was admissible under Article 29 of the Human Rights Act 1998.

The application was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The case was decided in favour of the applicant, who had been granted legal aid. The Government was represented by their Agent, Ms A. Sornarajah, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The decision was made to uphold the application.

In 2005 the applicant was convicted of rape. He was originally sentenced to life imprisonment with a tariff of five years. Upon appeal, this was reduced to a sentence of imprisonment for public protection. A few months prior to tariff expiry, the Secretary of State referred the applicant’s case to the Parole Board, pursuant to section 239(2) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003. The panel, which included a psychologist and a psychiatrist among their number, noted the recommendations for open conditions made by report writers, but also noted the identification of remaining areas of treatment need. They feared that there had been an underestimate of risk ... and an insufficient attention to the sadistic elements of the offences in other assessments.

The applicant’s tariff expired on 18 December 2008, by which time no Parole Board review had taken place. As a result of the number of cases awaiting oral hearing, the earliest available hearing date was in May. The hearing was eventually rescheduled for September 2009. The applicant challenged, by way of judicial review proceedings, the delay in fixing a Parole board hearing. The High Court handed down its judgment in the High Court case on 23 June 2009. In the context of the judicial review case, the ParoleBoard accepted that because of the inability to have the hearing in May, there had been a breach of Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

It is not now appropriate for any prisoner to take proceedings against the Parole Board alleging breaches of Article 5(4) unless there are very special circumstances. It will not be helpful, either to the prisoner or to the court, if claims are brought which in reality, because of the existing situation, are not likely to achieve any sensible redress and merely add to costs. The applicant was advised by his counsel that no appeal would be successful as the Court of Appeal would be bound to conclude that it could not prioritise any individual case. The court welcomes the steps that are clearly being taken now to ensure that that situation does not continue.

Of course, one has sympathy with those who may stay in prison longer than they perhaps, on one view, ought to. But, equally, the court cannot do the impossible. We cannot make orders which are only going to create difficulties for others and are not in any way desirable.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that he did not have a speedy review of the lawfulness of his detention, in violation of Article 5 of the convention. He was originally sentenced to life imprisonment with a tariff (i.e. minimum term to be served before eligibility for release arose) of five years. Upon appeal, this was reduced to a sentence of imprisonment for public protection (“IPP” – see paragraphs 22-23 below), which is also an indeterminate sentence. The application was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The Parole Board agreed to hold an oral hearing in the applicant’s case. The earliest available hearing date was in May. The hearing was eventually rescheduled for September 2009. The applicant challenged, by way of judicial review proceedings, the delay in fixing a Parole. Board accepted that because of the inability to have the hearing in May and the delay until September, there had been a breach of Article 5. § 4 of the Convention in that the hearing had not taken place speedily. The Secretary of State, however, did not accept that there was a breach. The Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the applicant. The High Court handed down its judgment in the judicial review proceedings on 23 June 2009. The judge outlined the background to the applicant’s claim, as follows: “4. a breach, having regard in particular to the fact that the pre-tariff advisory opinion of the Parole Board had effectively made it clear there was no chance of release upon expiry of the tariff’” The judge considered that it followed ‘inevitably’ from it that the panel, if asked, would not conceivably have directed the applicant's release. This meant that the hearing was delayed further than otherwise it need have been. Article 5(4) requires a speedy hearing to determine the lawfulness of the detention. 'Speedy' does not indicate a particular period, and I accept entirely that it is fact sensitive. In this case the cause has been the lack of man power in the Parole Board which has meant that it has been unable to provide the necessary panel, which in the case of a lifer and in deciding questions of possible release because it is said that the individual is no longer dangerous, has to be a panel headed by a judicial member. He concluded that the September 2008 advisory opinion in the applicant’s case could not address the question whether the post-tariff detention was lawful. However, any breach would not require payment of damages. The judge agreed with the decision not to pursue the claim for such an order. He said it would be inappropriate for an individual, seeking judicial review, to ‘jump the queue’ at the expense of those who did not seek judicial review. The applicant’s legal representative accepted that it was “not of the greatest importance” whether a declaration was granted or not. The judge decided: “In all the circumstances I do not think that it is necessary for me to make any formal declaration in the circumstances of this case.” The judge recorded that there was a breach, but it is a breach that will not provide, for this particular claimant, any great advantage. Judge notes that the measures put in place to alleviate the problem will not have immediate effect. ‘The delays continue and the backlog has not improved,’ he says. � ‘It is not now appropriate for any prisoner to take proceedings against the Parole Board alleging breaches of Article 5(4) unless there are very special circumstances.’ ‘We cannot make orders which are only going to create difficulties for others and are not in any way desirable, because, as I have already said, it is not helpful that prisoner A gets relief which may advance him in the queue but which inevitably means that prisoner B has a longer wait’ The applicant was advised by his counsel that no appeal would be successful as the Court of Appeal would be bound to conclude that it could not prioritise any individual case. The court welcomes the steps that are clearly being taken now to ensure that that situation does not continue. In. special circumstances, claims of this nature should now be discouraged. But, this has at least brought home to the court, and enabled the court to make the point, that the situation that existed was unsatisfactory, potentially contrary to law, and the court welcomes. the steps which are being taken to ensure it doesn’t happen again. The applicant was released from prison in September 2009. The Parole Board recommended that the applicant be moved to open conditions.

The authorities found the interior of the home completely destitute; there was hardly any furniture and there was no electricity or running water. On the following day, the applicant was committed to compulsory psychiatric care in accordance with the Act on Compulsory Psychiatric Care (Lagen om psykiatrisk tvångsvård, 1991:1128). The applicant claimed that she was not ill but agreed to the placement of the children in the temporary family home. A week later, she was released from psychiatric care and returned to her home. The Social Council applied to the County Administrative Court for a permanent care order in respect of all three children. The council maintained that the applicant had shown a serious lack of ability to care for her children. In its view, the children’s behaviour showed that their development had already been harmed. Since the applicant did not agree to voluntary care, it was necessary to take the children into public care on a permanent basis. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten) in Sundsvall. On 9 January 2006 the Administrative court of Appeal upheld the lower court's judgment in full. The children were placed in three different family homes, all within approximately 50 km of Skellefteå, as one family was not able to provide the care and support that each child needed. The applicant had contact rights to visit T. for one hour, once every other week, and spoke with her on the telephone once a week. She met S. once every third week in the presence of the social services. In May 2006 the applicant moved to live with her sister in Göteborg, located approximately 1,100 km from SkelLEFteå. In November 2006 the. applicant, through her legal counsel, requested the Social Council to allow her more time with her children as she felt that the children. were being deprived of contact with her. The children had suffered severe harm to their health and development because of the deficiencies in the applicant’s ability to care for them. The Social Council concluded in its investigation report that the children had a right to contact with their mother but that their best interests required that the contact be limited in order to ensure their secure and positive development. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court and requested that she be granted contact rights to her children much more often than only twice a year. She could see no reason for such restricted contact and found it to be contrary to the best interests of the children as they would forget their mother. The children had lived with her until May 2005 and they had had a close and warm relationship. The Social Council contested the appeal. It submitted that the children were currently in the process of developing and learning things that they had not had the opportunity to learn before. It noted that the last meeting between the applicant and her children, on 23 January 2007, had passed without incident, partly because eight adults had been present to ensure the children’s well-being. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Administrative Court of Appeal, maintaining her claims and adding that she wished to see her children at least once a month in order to ensure that they would not forget her. She felt that the family home parents had a negative attitude towards her and that this influenced the children. The Social Council had observed that despite the applicant’s visits having been planned and very structured, the children had still had negative reactions before and after each meeting. The applicant appealed to the Administrative Court of Appeal, maintaining that she wanted contact rights with her children during one weekend per month, without the presence of others. The Social Council contested the appeal and maintained the reasons set forth in its decision. The court found that with the support of the Social Council and the family homes during the meetings, these could be increased to four times per year for the applicant. In its view, this would provide the children with a good contact with their mother while not jeopardising their continued development. The Social Council wanted to know if the applicant suffered from a disorder or mental illness. It recommended supplementary examinations and made a number of proposals for supportive measures, including establishing fixed structures and routines in her daily life. It was also stressed that this specific impairment of her capabilities could hardly be sufficient to “disqualify her as a parent’ The Administrative Court of Appeal upheld the lower court’s judgment in full. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 36144/09) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was born in 1974 and lives in Diyarbakır. In the course of a military operation, several terrorists were killed by the security forces in Bingöl. On 28 March 2006 a large group of people assembled at their funeral and protested against the security Forces. About 1,500 to 2,000 people resisted the police, attacking them with stones, blocking the traffic by burning tyres and damaging nearby shops and public buildings by throwing stones. Many demonstrators were arrested by the police. On 2 May 2006 the Diyarbakır Public Prosecutor issued an indictment charging the applicant with involvement in the activities of an illegal organisation. The applicant was convicted in May 2007 and sentenced to six years and three months' imprisonment. On 30 May 2011 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court and the applicant was sentenced to a further six years in prison. The appeal against the conviction was dismissed on 27 October 2008 on the ground that the complainant’s statement had not been taken by the police. In the meantime, on the basis of the medical reports, the applicant filed a complaint alleging ill-treatment by police officers. He also alleged that the doctor who had not found any new traces of ill- treatment was guilty of professional misconduct.

It was proposed to instigate contacts between the child and her parents under psychotherapeutic or pedagogical guidance. The divorce was decreed on that same day. She can also see her mother when she needs to. She was also able to visit her brother and sister when she wants. She now has full contact with both her mother and father. She no longer needs to go to the foster home when she visits with her brother or sister. On 5 March 2002 the applicant requested that a court decision be given immediately. District Court considered that the applicant was unable to accept the child’s wishes and her present life circumstances within the foster family. Under Civil Procedure Rules, which came into force on 26 April 1999, hearings, including those in small claims cases, are to be held in public. There is a discretion for the court to hold a hearing in private where: (a) publicity would defeat the object of the hearing; (b) it involves matters relating to national security; (c) it is confidential information (including information relating to personal financial matters) and publicity would damage that confidentiality; (d) a private hearing is necessary to protect the interests of any child or person suffering from mental incapacity; or it is a hearing of an application made without notice and it would be unjust to the respondent.

The sum of the dispute and the nature of. the dispute were basically no different from the usual “run of the mill“ arbitration disputes heard in. any county court. The case was not contested before the Court, as found by the Commission. Mr Scarth then applied for leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal alleging a lack of public hearing, misconduct by the judge and an overall unfairness of the proceedings. Mr Scarth was heard in open court and leave was refused on 9 November 1995. Lord Justice Morritt noted that the “European Convention on Human Rights is not part of our law in the way the European Community law is“. He refused the application on 9 May 1995 and made a costs order against Mr Sc Barth. These costs were subsequently assessed at GBP 1,032.76. They are being appealed in the European Court of Human Rights. Under the Civil Procedure Rules, which came into force on 26 April 1999, hearings, including those in small claims cases, are to be held in public. There is a discretion for the court to hold a hearing in private where: (a) publicity would defeat the object of the hearing; (b) it involves matters relating to national security; (c) it is confidential information and publicity would damage that confidentiality; (d) a private hearing is necessary to protect the interests of any child or person suffering from mental incapacity; or it is a hearing of an application made without notice and it would be unjust to the respondent for there to be a public hearing.

The applicants requested the court to dismiss two experts who took part in the preparation of a report, alleging that these experts were not impartial since they were civil servants. On 29 December 1997 the First Instance Court awarded the applicants a certain amount of additional compensation. On 9 May 2000 the Gebze Civil Court of First Instances decided that the plot was of rural nature.

The applicant was born in 1977 and lives in Istanbul. On 28 June 2003 two police officers went to the Beşiktaş district of Istanbul following a complaint by a woman, and imposed an administrative fine on a taxi driver. Subsequently, the policemen and the taxi driver commenced a verbal dispute in the presence of the applicant. The applicant told the police officers that he would pay the fine on his friend’s behalf. The police officers then pushed the applicant to the ground, handcuffed him and began kicking and punching him. He was subsequently put in the police car. One of the officers closed the car door on the applicant's leg. According to a medical report issued following X-rays and an orthopaedic examination, his right leg was broken as a result of the incident.

The case involves the arrest of an Austrian man on suspicion of using a stolen credit card. The applicant and Mr and Mrs Hauser sought compensation for the pecuniary damage sustained on account of their detention. The courts refused their compensation claims on the ground that, contrary to the requirements of the 1969 Act, the suspicion concerning them had not been dispelled. The case was settled in 1992 and the applicant was released from detention on 19 July 1992. The proceedings were later discontinued after a graphologist found that it was unlikely that the signatures on the payment slips for the purchases made with the stolen card were in Mr Werner’s hand.

The Government granted the application and allowed the construction of the railway in the proposed “corridor” under the condition, inter alia, that the NRA adopt a railway plan before 1 July 2009 and also a specific plan for the realisation of the necessary environmental compensation measures. The plan on compensation measures had to be presented to the government on 12 June 2003. The application was granted on 15 October 1999.

The NRA applied to the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen) in the County of Västerbotten for a permit to construct the railway in the specific Natura 2000 area. The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the petitions for a judicial review because it was not possible to determine who should be considered an interested party. The exact route of the railway would not be established until the railway plan had been drawn up. Until then, it could not be assessed with any certainty who would be affected to the extent that they were entitled to bring an action. One judge dissented, finding that the issue of locus standi in respect of each petitioner should be further investigated in order to ensure that the individual interests were taken into account.

The Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the petitions for a judicial review because it was not possible to determine who should be considered an interested party at that stage of the railway planning. One judge dissented, finding that the issue of locus standi in respect of each petitioner should be further investigated by the court in order to ensure that the individual interests were taken into account, having regard to the binding character of the Government’s decision in the later railway planning proceedings.

The NRA applied for a permit to build a railway in a Natura 2000 area. The Government said that the activity could be permitted, despite its harmful effect on the environment. Three property owners petitioned the Supreme Administrative Court for a judicial review of the case and requested that the Government’s decision be quashed. But the court dismissed the petitions because it was not possible to determine who should be considered an interested party at that stage of the railway planning. The exact route would not be established until the railway plan had been drawn up. Until then, it could not be assessed with any certainty who would be affected to the extent that they were entitled to bring an action.

County Administrative Board granted a construction permit for the railway by a decision of 14 October 2004, which was subsequently appealed against to the Environmental Court. The Environmental Court decided to examine the cases jointly. By judgments of 24 May 2005 and 13 June 2005, considering itself bound by the Government’s decision of 12 June 2003 on the permissibility of the railway project, the court decided to grant all the permits requested by the NRA. By a judgment of 6 December 2007, the Environmental Court of Appeal affirmed the binding nature of the Government's decision. On 9 May 2008 the Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) refused leave to appeal and, thus, the Environmental court's judgment became final.

County Administrative Board granted a construction permit for the railway by a decision of 14 October 2004, which was subsequently appealed against to the Environmental Court. The Environmental Court decided to examine the cases jointly. The court considered itself bound by the Government’s decision as to the permissibility of the railway project and thus limited its examination to the environmental compensation measures. All applicants except Mr Osterman appealed against the part which concerned the permit to construct the bridges. The Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) refused leave to appeal and, thus, the Supreme Court's judgment became final on 9 May 2008. The decision of 6 December 2007 affirmed the binding nature of the Government's decision and approved the construction.

The County Administrative Board granted a construction permit for the railway by a decision of 14 October 2004. The decision was subsequently appealed against to the Environmental Court. The Environmental Court decided to examine the cases jointly. It found that the Government’s decision had not contained a detailed examination of measures necessary to compensate for environmental harm caused by the railway project. The Supreme Court (Högsta domstolen) refused leave to appeal and, thus, the Environmental court's judgment became final in May 2008. The Supreme Administrative Court rejected the petition, finding that the railway plan was in line with the Government’s decision of 12 June 2003. The court considered that the question of permissibility of a railway project was within the power of the Government, which had to take into account public interests such as environmental, industrial, economic and regional policy. It found that the specific stretch chosen in the rail plan was situated within the permitted “corridor” and thus rejected the appeals. The decision was binding for the subsequent proceedings in that courts and other decision-making bodies could not examine issues that had been determined by that decision.

All of the applicants and several other petitioners turned to the Supreme Administrative Court and requested that it, by way of a judicial review, order the quashing of the Government’s decision. They claimed, inter alia, that, although their civil rights were affected by the planned railway, they had not had these rights considered and determined by a court, in violation of the Convention. They also asserted that the chosen location of the railway was contrary to provisions of the Environmental Code and the EU Habitats Directive. The court found that the specific stretch chosen in the railway plan was situated within the permitted “corridor” and thus rejected the appeals.

The fact that the court, on 1 December 2004, had concluded that no individual petitioner could be considered to have locus standi in relation to the railway project had also not been considered.

One judge dissented, considering that the Supreme Administrative Court’s judgment contravened its decision of 1 December 2004. She noted, inter alia, that the adoption of a railway plan – as opposed to the construction permits – had direct consequences for the individual as it entailed a right for the railway company, under certain conditions, to expropriate land. At least ten of the applicants have received some form of compensation as a consequence of the railway construction, either for land requisitioned or for reduced residential value. In the vicinity of some properties, whose owners have not received compensation, noise barriers have been erected in order to keep the noise from the railway below the applicable target values.

The court should have examined all the objections presented by the appellants, including the claim that there were better alternative locations for the railway. It is not clear whether the other applicants requested compensation.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 29878/09) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged, in particular, that they had been denied effective access to court in relation to decisions taken on the construction of a railway, in violation of their rights under Articles 6 and 8 of the convention. The application was communicated to the Government on 21 May 2012. The case was heard on 7 June 2013 and the verdict was delivered on 9 June 2013. The decision was handed down on 11 June 2014 and the decision was made to dismiss the application. The proposed railway construction concerned certain areas which were or were going to be part of Natura 2000. The Government stated, inter alia, that the activity could be permitted, despite its harmful effect on the environment. The property owners claimed that the decision contradicted Swedish law as well as applicable European Union law, including the Habitats Directive. A number of individual property owners, including three of the applicants in the present case, petitioned the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten) for a judicial review of the case and requested that the Government’s decision be quashed. The case was heard by the Supreme Court of Sweden on 7 January 2011. NRA applied to the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen) in the County of Västerbotten for a permit to construct the railway in the specific Natura 2000 area. They also asked the Environmental Court (miljödomstolen) in Umeå for permits to build two bridges. Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the petitions for a judicial review because it was not possible to determine who should be considered an interested party at that stage of the railway planning. Environmental Court decided to examine the cases jointly. By judgments of 24 May 2005 and 13 June 2005, considering itself bound by the Government’s decision of 12 June 2003, the court decided to grant all the permits requested. In 2005 the NRA adopted a railway plan for the area in question. 12 applicants appealed to the Government against the railway plan. In 2007 the Environmental Court granted the permits requested by the NRA. In 2008 the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal the decision. The Supreme Administrative Court rejected the petition to quash the Government’s decision to build the railway. The railway plan was approved with certain added conditions. The decision on the construction of the railway was upheld by the European Court of Human Rights in December 2008. The case was heard by the Swedish High Court of Justice in December 2007. The High Court found that the rail plan was in line with the European Convention on Human Rights and EU Habitats Directive. Government had not been obliged to review its decision of 12 June 2003 on the permissibility of the railway project and the designation of the “corridor” in which the railway could be located. These issues could not be examined in the third stage of the decision process. The adoption of a railway plan – as opposed to the construction permits – had direct consequences for the individual as it entailed a right for the railway company, under certain conditions, to expropriate land. The court, in the instant case, should have examined all the objections presented by the appellants, including the claim that there were better alternative locations. According to the dissenting judge, a full judicial review had also been foreseen by the court. At least ten of the applicants have received some form of compensation as a consequence of the railway construction. In one case, the change to noise-reducing windows was partly paid by the NRA. In the vicinity of some properties, whose owners have not received compensation, noise barriers have been erected in order to keep the noise from the railway below the applicable target values. It is not clear whether the other applicants requested compensation. The case was heard by the High Court of the Supreme Court in Dublin on February 7 and 8 this year. The court was told that the railway was to be built on land requisitioned or for reduced residential value or market value.

The applicant was charged with attempted murder and making threats to kill. The Crown case was that D.G. had been summoned to the scene by the applicant and another co-accused using a mobile telephone belonging to M.H. The applicant denied the charges, alleging that he had left the scene at an early stage and gone to a neighbouring house. He accepted that eye witness evidence and CCTV recordings demonstrated he had used a telephone at certain points. However, he said that he was a drug dealer using his own telephone and that the calls were made for his own criminal purposes and were nothing to do with the summoning of D. G.

An argument broke out between the applicant and D.M. in a residential street on 30 May 2004. Within about half an hour of the dispute, a third man, D.G., arrived at the scene equipped with a loaded shotgun and shot D.m. in the back of the head. The applicant denied the charges, alleging that he had left the scene at an early stage and gone to a neighbouring house. The Crown contended that the applicant could be seen making certain calls. There was also eye witness evidence of him making at least one of the critical calls. He is currently detained in HMP Lowdham Grange, Nottingham.

Crown case involved video recordings from closed circuit television (CCTV) cameras near the scene. Crown contended that the applicant could be seen making certain calls. In total, the Crown case was that six relevant calls were made from M.H.'s mobile telephone to D.G. or one of his associates. The applicant denied the Crown contention that it showed him making a call at a relevant time. He accepted that eye witness evidence and CCTV recordings demonstrated that he had used a telephone at certain points. However, he said that he was a drug dealer using his own telephone and that the calls were making for his own criminal purposes. The jury asked for the CCTV footage to be shown to them again in court. The judge agreed and said they could watch it in the jury room if they wanted. The jury retired after the second day of deliberations. The court convened with junior counsel for the applicant among those attending. The only issue that arises as a result of the CCTV request is who exactly is present in court when they view the material. It is a matter that we have discussed between counsel, and of course, subject to your Lordship's view, I think the general view is that if they are able to watch it on their own, it would be much more constructive – if counsel and your Lordships were not present. The judge instructed the jury to return and directed them as follows: “We are going to leave [Officer M] in this court with you, and he will play any part of the video that you have seen,” he said. “There is to be no other communication with him – or any communication from him – than simply asking him to play you what you want to see – and I think it is probably better,’ the judge added. No assent was recorded from junior counsel for the applicant but no objections were raised to the course of action proposed. The jury returned to the dock and the trial continued. Jury was left alone in the court room with Officer M at 2.05 p.m. to begin reviewing the video evidence. The jury spent almost two hours viewing the video recordings in the presence of Officer M. When the court reconvened, leading counsel for the applicant directed the judge's attention to various authorities, including Archbold's Criminal Pleading, Evidence and Practice. The judge agreed to reconvene at 4 p.M. as he did not wish to interrupt the jury's viewing of the video footage. The hearing was adjourned at 3.30 p.n. and will resume at 10 a.m next week. The judge subsequently advised the jury as follows: “We have reconsidered the procedure for your viewing [the CCTV] footage, and in order to give you complete freedom for discussion amongst yourselves as you view that footage" The jury viewed the video recordings alone for about an hour. Anthony Tyrer pleaded guilty to unlawful assault in March 1972. The applicant was sentenced on the same day to three strokes of the birch. He appealed against sentence to the Staff of Government Division of the High Court of Justice of the Isle of Man. The appeal was heard and dismissed on the afternoon of 28 April 1972; the court considered that an unprovoked assault occasioning actual bodily harm was always very serious and that there were no reasons for interfering with the sentence. The birching raised, but did not cut, the applicant’s skin and he was sore for about a week and a half afterwards. Mr. Tyrer was made to take down his trousers and underpants and bend over a table; he was held by two policemen whilst a third administered the punishment.

The instrument used to inflict the punishment is a birch rod of the following dimensions: Length from end of handle to tip of spray 40 inches, Circumference of handle at top of binding 3 1/2 inches. In the case of a child who is under the age of 14, a light cane not exceeding half an inch in diameter will be used. The punishment is to be inflicted on the child in the presence of an officer of higher rank, and if the child is a young person, the officer must be present. The sentence must be carried out within six months of the date of the punishment. The child must be of legal age, and not older than 14 years of age.

The sentence was governed by the following provisions: (a) the instrument used shall, in the case of a child, be a cane, and in any other case shall be a birch rod. (b) the number of strokes to be inflicted is not more than six. (c) the punishment must be inflicted privately as soon as possible after the sentence has been handed down. The punishment must not be inflicted in the presence of a parent or other officer of higher rank than a constable. The sentence must also not be imposed after six months have passed since the sentence was given. The penalty should not be more than a fine of £1,000 or a prison term of up to two years.

No representations from the applicant were recorded as having been made. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 55434/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. By a decision of 25 October 2005, the Court declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine), the parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The Court ruled that the application was admissible and that the parties had a right to respond to it in writing. A certificate dated 6 November 1999 and signed by the applicant confirms that the applicant received the pamphlet “The Rights of a Soldier Charged with an Offence under the Army Act 1955” and that he had had the opportunity to be advised by an officer of his choice. The final report dated 7 February 2000 recorded for the first time an additional charge against the applicant pursuant to section 70 of the 1955 Act: rape contrary to section 1(1) of the Sexual Offences Act 1956. The applicant. was given a four-page document immediately before that hearing, which document was taken back from him. immediately thereafter. A short note by the CO (“referred to Higher Authority”) constitutes the sole record before the Court of that hearing. No reasons were noted as to why the applicant had been detained except in the last form (dated 7 February 2000) which recorded the same reasons as in the above-noted 8-day reports. It is undesirable in the interests of discipline that he should be at large or consort with his comrades. A Special Report, dated 10 January 2000 and completed by a lieutenant colonel (chief of staff) of Headquarters Land Command, recorded that approval had been given for the continued detention of the applicant. The applicant's representative applied for a writ of habeas corpus to the High Court. The application was served on the CO of the MCTC on 19 February 2000. He was posted to the 47th Regiment Royal Artillery. The applicant and his two co-defendants were tried by Army General Court Martial on a joint charge of rape between 14 May and 25 May 2001. The applicant was posted with immediate effect to a different unit in a different country namely the UK, and issued with specific orders preventing him from being able to influence the witnesses. He was charged with rape and indecent assault, but was found not guilty of either charge. The case was adjourned for two years, but the applicant was allowed to remain in the Army. He has since been released from the Army and returned to the UK. He is now serving in the British Army as a private.

The applicant alleged that the length of his detention was excessive and that the criminal proceedings in his case exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of the convention. The application was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The case was decided in favour of the applicant and the Polish Government. The decision was based on a reasonable suspicion, confirmed by testimonies of the victims and of other suspects, that the applicant had committed the offences. In October 1999 the public prosecutor ordered expert opinions on the kind of injuries the victims had suffered. The opinions were submitted on 6 and 15 October 1999. The court found that the grounds for detention on remand were still valid and owing to the fact that the crimes had been committed in co-operation with other persons, there remained a high risk that the applicant might interfere with the course of justice and exert pressure on witnesses and victims. The courts also pointed to the necessity of separating the suspects. The case involved thirteen defendants and sixty-six witnesses. The hearing scheduled for 30 January 2001 was adjourned in order to have one of the victims heard with the assistance of a psychologist. From 11 April 2001 until 10 April 2002 the applicant served a one-year prison sentence imposed in separate proceedings. It was proved that two of the defendants had exerted improper pressure on witnesses and thus caused them to alter significantly their versions of the events. Several witnesses had changed their testimonies and the reading out of their earlier statements had been justified. Almost thirty witnesses remained to be heard at that stage of the proceedings and there was a need to summon further witnesses. Fines were imposed on eleven absent witnesses. The applicant's detention was prolonged until 15 February 2002. The court noted that, since June 2000, the first-instance court had held seven hearings and examined ten witnesses. The absence of other witnesses was the major reason for the prolongation of the proceedings. The trial court had taken proper measures to speed up the trial. The examination of the witnesses had been very time-consuming owing to the complexity of the case and the mental state of the victims. The parties had also requested additional witnesses to be heard. and to cross-examine them. From 10 April 2002 until 9 December 2002 the applicant was serving a prison sentence imposed on him in separate proceedings. The applicant was sentenced to nine years' imprisonment and a four-year period of deprivation of his civic rights. The court dismissed the defendant's request to summon other absent witnesses, having found that their examination would not add anything to the case. On 29 April 2005 the Court of Appeal dismissed the complaint as ill-founded. The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant's cassation appeal on 11 March 2005. The investigation has produced sufficient indicative evidence to suggest that Mr Apostolos Mangouras could be criminally responsible for the offences in question. Amongst those discs found in the former’s house, certain allegedly contained separatist propaganda. On the same day, the İdil public prosecutor extended the period of the applicants’ detention as requested. The applicants all maintained that they had been in their homes at the time of the incident and had had no involvement in the armed attack. Yetgin Adırbelli, Gülek AdıRbelli and Mehmet Goran did not request a lawyer. The applicants were brought before the İdil public prosecutor. Yetgin Adırbelli had been arrested on suspicion of being in possession of a firearm and there had been an investigation in respect of Metin Goran as he had been suspected of forgery. On 12 March 2003 the public prosecutor at the Diyarbakır State Security Court issued a decision not to prosecute, on the ground that there was insufficient evidence to initiate criminal proceedings against the applicants. The case originated in an application (no. 8790/79) against Austria lodged with the Commission on 19 September 1979 under Article 25. The purpose of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1. The applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent her (Rule 30). The applicant filed her claims under Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention. The hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Government filed a document during the course of the hearings. The Court heard addresses by Mr. Türk and Mr. Matzka for the Government, by Mr Ermacora for the Commission and by. Proksch for the applicant, as well as their replies to its questions. On 27 March, the Court decided on 27 March that the proceedings should continue without resumption of the proceedings (Rule 26) The Government also replied to two supplementary questions which the Registrar had addressed to them. The applicant, who is a United States citizen, lives in Munich in the Federal Republic of Germany. Wishing to build a holiday residence in Hopfgarten, a village in the Austrian Tyrol, she approached, with the assistance of municipal officials, the owners of a plot of land which had until then been used for agricultural purposes. Sale negotiations began in 1971 and apparently led, in 1973, to an initial contract. One year later, Mrs. Sramek paid to the vendors the greater part of the agreed price. However, the definitive contract was not drawn up until 13 January 1977. The contract could not take effect unless it were approved by the local Real Property Transactions Authority (Grundverkehrsbehörde) On 3 June 1977, the Regional Real Property Transactions Authority at the Government Office of the Tyrol held a hearing. The applicant received a copy of the appeal but did not file any observations in reply. The contract in question was therefore contrary to social and economic interests within the meaning of the above-mentioned Act. There were, in fact, already 110 foreign landowners in Hopfgarten and it could be seen from a series of decisions of the Regional Authority that this municipality was one of those where the danger of foreign domination was imminent. The parties, namely the Transactions Officer and Mrs. Sramek, were present. The latter appeared in person, without the assistance of a lawyer. According to the minutes of the hearing, the rapporteur presented the facts and read out the expert opinions. The owner of the land had already made a first payment of 111,591 schillings. The Authority noted that there were 110 foreign landowners in Hopfgarten, owning 5.6 hectares of land. The proportion of non-Austrian owners already exceeded 10 per cent and the extent of their holdings revealed a tendency towards foreign domination. According to the Authority, experience showed that the approval of a contract between a landowner and a foreigner led to an influx of other foreigners who also wished to buy land in the locality. This caused prices to rise substantially, making it very difficult, if not impossible, for the indigenous population to find housing for themselves. Mrs Sramek was intending to use the land in question for the construction of a holiday residence. The acquisition contemplated was therefore prejudicial to economic and social interests and thus fell foul of, in particular, section 4(2)(a) of the 1970/1973 Act. The Regional Authority rejected the applicant’s argument that she had already concluded a contract in 1973, that is at a time when American citizens were treated on an equal footing with Austrians. The Authority emphasised firstly that it had to base itself on the factual and legal situation obtaining at the time when the decision had to be taken. In its view, the 1928 treaty had not established any equality between citizens of the two States. Mrs. Sramek alleged that the Regional Authority had applied section 4(2)(a) of the 1970/1973 Act in a misconceived (denkunmöglich) manner. On these grounds, she requested the Constitutional Court to annul the decision under appeal or, in the alternative, to refer the case to the Administrative Court. The Constitutional Court dismissed the appeal on 3 March 1979 (Erkenntnisse und Beschlüsse des Verfassungsgerichtshofes, 1979, vol. 44, no. 8501) It took the view that the. Regional Authority was indeed a “tribunal’ within the meaning of Article 6 (art. 6) of. the Convention and gave decisions which the executive could neither annul nor vary. The plot in question was sold to an Austrian who, according to the Government, turned it back into grazing-land. The Regional Authority had taken the view that it could examine the new contract, provided that its decision was held in abeyance pending the outcome of the Constitutional Court’s proceedings. The Constitutional Court sat in camera and gave judgment without holding a hearing. Most of the Länder have enacted legislation whereby all contracts relating to agricultural or forestry land and also, in some cases, real property transactions with foreigners have to be approved by special authorities. If approval is withheld, the acquisition is null and void (section 16(1)). The decisions of the Farm Commission are taken by majority vote. They are subject to appeal to the Regional Authority (see paragraph 24 below) The Transactions Officer, who is appointed for three years by the Government of the Tyrol, must be a person who is experienced in real property transaction matters. His secretariat is provided by a division of the Office of the said Government. If the case is referred to it, the Regional Real Property Transactions Authority takes a decision as the second and final instance. Its membership varies according to the subject-matter of the contract to be examined. In the case of agricultural or forestry land - whether the buyer be Austrian or foreign - its voting members are (section 13(4), no. 1): “(a) a person experienced inReal Property transaction matters, who shall act as chairman; (b) a member of the judiciary (Richterstand) In 1973, the Constitutional Court held that the Act did not fix the duration of the members’ term of office. It also did not lay down the circumstances in which members might be removed from office. Following this judgment, the Tyrolean legislature amended, by the same Act, the provisions in section 13 concerning, inter alia, exercise of the office of member of the Regional Authority. The Act also gave the Government the power of appointing the members (save for a judge, who was appointed by the Federal Minister of Justice) The Act of 28 November 1973 was then amended on 25 November 1973. The result is that the Regional Real Property Transactions Authority now has a three-year term. Members of the Real Property Transactions Authorities receive for their work remuneration and a travel allowance. The parties are entitled to consult the case-file (section 17) and must be given an opportunity of presenting their arguments (section 37) The competent authority may decide to hold a hearing (section 39(2), which will not take place in public. In certain circumstances which may give reason to doubt his impartiality, the civil servant concerned must arrange to be replaced (section 7). The parties have the right to be heard (rechtliches Gehör) and, inter alia, to adduce their arguments and evidence. The Government of the Tyrol issued rules of procedure for the Real Property Transactions Authorities in 1966. Under Article 3 para. 1, the Authorities shall deliberate and vote in the absence of the parties, if appropriate after oral hearings. The right to consult the case-file (Akteneinsicht), guaranteed by Article 17 of the General Administrative Procedure Act, does not extend. Decisions of a Regional Authority may be challenged before the Constitutional Court but not before the Administrative Court. The case was still pending before the domestic courts when the applicant died on 14 June 2005. The Constitution was amended on 18 June 1999 and the military judge sitting on the bench was replaced by a civilian judge. The applicant's final defence submissions had not been submitted to the court when his case was separated from the file. In the course of the proceedings the State security Court rejected the applicant's requests for release, taking into account the nature of the alleged offence and the state of the evidence. The court ruled that the case should be separated as it was not clear whether the applicant had committed the offence.

The applicant was injured by gunfire during arrest. He received a single bullet to his lower left leg. A cap gun (a toy gun that creates a loud sound akin to a gunshot and a puff of smoke when the trigger is pulled) had been found in the applicant's possession. The ballistics examination of the cap gun and eight cartridges found that the 99 mm. semi automatic cap gun fired noise and gas caps. The bullet trajectory was established as having entered from the back of the leg and exited from the front. The applicant had suffered a fracture of the fibula (small bone located on the outside of the lower leg) The applicant received medical treatment at Kartal State Hospital.

The European Union’s Convention on Human Rights was passed in 1989. The law says that the right to a tax-free allowance is a fundamental right. The European Union has since amended the law to make sure that it applies to all citizens, not just those who live in the EU member states. However, the law has not been fully implemented, and the European Union is not obliged to implement the law as it stands. The EU has to make up the difference between what the law says and what it actually is, and this is not always the case. In this case, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the law doesn’t apply, and that it should be amended.

The law states that only women can claim an allowance when their child is born. The law was changed after the birth of the first baby in the United States in 1967. The act was passed to make up for the loss of an exemption from the law. The new law was enacted on 1 July 1986 and came into effect on 1 January 1987. It was amended again on 1 August 1989 to remove the provision for women to claim an annual allowance of up to £5,000 if they are married or have a child under the age of 18. The change was made by the European Court of Human Rights, but not by the Supreme Court of Justice.

The European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) was passed in 1990. It was supposed to be a treaty between the EU and member states. But the ECHR has now changed the law to say that it is not a treaty and can only be applied to certain cases. This means that it can be used to protect human rights. The ECHR can no longer be used as a tool for the protection of human rights, it can only protect the right to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. It can't be used for any other purpose than to protect the rights of the children of the European Union. This is why the ECHR was created. It will not be able to use it for other purposes.
