He appealed against that decision to the Vienna Regional Employment Office (Landesarbeitsamt) on the grounds that section 26(1) of the Unemployment Benefit Act 1977 was discriminatory and, therefore, unconstitutional. On 18 August 1989 he lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof) The case was heard in public in Strasbourg on 23 October 1997. The applicant's complaint was unfounded, seeing that the legislature had a certain amount of time in which to adapt new rules to changes in society. It added that even if regard was had to recent statutory amendments (section 26 of the Unemployment Benefit Act had been amended by a federal law of 12 December 1989 – see paragraph 15 below) The Constitutional Court held that section 26(1) did not infringe the applicant’s constitutional rights and was not contrary to Article 8 or Article 12 of the Convention. The complaint was rejected on the ground that it did not have sufficient prospects of success. The case was referred to the Court of Appeal.

The applicant and Mr Jensen, but not the three Greenjackets, appealed against the City Court’s judgment to the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret). The High Court, by five votes to one, dismissed the appeal. The Supreme Court (Højesteret), which by four votes toOne dismissed the Appeal in a judgment of 13 February 1989. The majority held: “The defendants have caused the publication of the racist statements made by a narrow circle of persons and thereby made those persons liable to punishment” The dissenting member was of the view that, although the statements by the GreenJackets constituted offences under Article 266 (b) of the Penal Code, they had not transgressed the bounds of the freedom of speech to be enjoyed by television.

The applicant had encouraged the Greenjackets to express their racist views, which, in so far as they were broadcast on television, in itself constituted a breach of Article 266 (b) of the Penal Code. The statements were broadcast without any counterbalancing comments, after the recordings had been edited by the applicant. eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 9 September 1993 by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and on 11 October 1993 by Denmark. It originated in an application (no. 15890/89) against Denmark lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Danish national, Mr Jens Olaf Jersild, on 25 July 1989. The object of the request and of the Government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10 of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent him (Rule 30). The case was heard by a Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights. The application was brought by Human Rights Watch, a New York based non-governmental human rights organisation. The hearing was adjourned until 20 April 1994, when it was expected to be heard again. The Commission produced a number of documents and two video-cassettes, as requested by the Registrar on the President’s instructions, and the applicant submitted further details on his claims under Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention. The applicant also showed the video-recording of the television programme in issue in his case to the judges taking part in the proceedings. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 April 1994. The Court heard addresses by Mr Rozakis, Mr Lehmann, Mr Elmer, Mr Boyle and Mr Trier, and also replies to a question put by the President. The applicant, Jens Olaf Jersild, a Danish national, is a journalist and lives in Copenhagen. He was at the time of the events giving rise to the present case, and still is, employed by Danmarks Radio (Danish Broadcasting Corporation), assigned to its Sunday News Magazine (Søndagsavisen) The latter is known as a serious television programme, dealing with a wide range of social and political issues, including xenophobia, immigration and refugees. Interview lasted between five and six hours, of which between two and two and a half hours were video-recorded. Danmarks Radio paid the interviewees fees in accordance with its usual practice. applicant subsequently edited and cut the film of the interview down to a few minutes. The transcript of the Greenjackets item reads as follows: "It’s good being a racist. We believe Denmark is for the Danes" "The flag on the wall is the flag of the Southern States from the American Civil War, but today it is also the symbol of racism" "I just ran into a petrol station with a ... gun and made them give me some money. Then I ran out again" I had a little fight with the police together with some friends. I was arrested for street violence. There are 20-25 young people from STUDSEN in the same group. They meet not far away from the public housing area near some old houses which are to be torn down. They met here to reaffirm among other things their racism, their hatred of immigrants and their support for the Ku Klux Klan. I think what they do is right. A nigger is not a human being, it’s an ape, man. People should be allowed to keep slaves, I think so anyway. You can also see that from their body structure, man, big flat noses, with cauliflower ears etc., man. Broad heads and very broad bodies, hairy, you are looking at a gorilla and compare it with an ape. Henrik is one of the strongest supporters of the Klan. He hates the foreign workers, ‘Perkere’ [a very derogatory word in Danish for immigrant workers]. ‘They come up here, man, and sponge on our society,’ he says. ‘We don’t like their mentality - I mean they can damn well, I mean ... what’s it called ... I mean if they feel like speaking Russian in their homes, right, then it's okay, but what we don't like is when they walk around in those Zimbabwe-clothes and then speak this hula-hula language in the street’ Per Axholt, known as ‘Pax’ [(P)], is employed in the youth centre in Studsgårdsgade. He has worked there for several years, but many give up a lot sooner because of the tough environment. He feels that the reasons why the young people are persecuting the immigrants is that they are themselves powerless and disappointed. What do you think they would say that they want, if you asked them? (P) Just what you and I want. Some control over their lives, work which may be considered decent and which they like, a reasonable economic situation, a reasonably functioning family, a wife or a husband and some children. The 'Perkere' have been pinching videos, where they have been our customers, so they have money. They have been told over a long period that the means by which to achieve success is money. If people want to be out here and have a nice time and be racists and drink beer, and have fun, then it’s quite obvious you don’t want to sit in the slammer. If you really get into the joint it would be such a ridiculously ridiculous story. You would have to be a crazy person to get into it. There are no bad consequences, so probably that's why they do it, so it's not prison that doesn't frighten people. No complaints were made to the Radio Council, which had competence in such matters, or to Danmarks Radio but the Bishop of Ålborg complained to the Minister of Justice. The Public Prosecutor instituted criminal proceedings in the City Court of Copenhagen (Københavns Byret) against the three youths. “Just take a picture of a gorilla, man, and then look at a nigger, it’s a gorilla.“ “... the Northern States wanted that the niggers should be free human beings, man. Three Greenjackets were convicted of making racist statements on TV. The applicant was convicted of aiding and abetting them, as was Mr Jensen, in his capacity as programme controller. The High Court dismissed the appeal by five votes to one. The applicant and Mr Jensen appealed from the High Court judgment to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) The Supreme Court, which by four votes toone dismissed the Appeal in a judgment of 13 February 1989. The majority found: “The defendants have caused the publication of the racist statements made by a narrow circle of persons and thereby made those persons liable to punishment” The majority also found that the defendants violated Article 266 (b) in conjunction with Article 23 of the Penal Code. The dissenting member was of the view that, although the statements by the Greenjackets constituted offences, they had not transgressed the bounds of the freedom of speech to be enjoyed by television. Supreme Court ruled in favour of the defendants’ acquittal. The majority had attached importance to the fact that they had caused the racist statements to be made public. The statements, which would hardly have been punishable under Article 266 (b) of the Penal Code had they not been made to a wide circle (“videre kreds’) of people, became clearly punishable as they were broadcast on television. Their news or information value was not such as to justify their dissemination and therefore did not warrant acquitting the defendants. This did not mean that extremist views could not be reported in the press, but such reports must be carried out in a more balanced and comprehensive manner than was the case in the television programme. Also, Justice Hermann pointed out that the application of the measures was a matter of law, and not of a political nature, and was therefore not subject to the legal scrutiny it would have received in a democratic society. The decision was made by a majority of 8 to 1, with the minority voting for the application to be rejected.

The applicants, a married couple of Iraqi origin, were born in 1957 and 1963 respectively and live in Västerås. They rented a flat in Rinkeby, a suburb of Stockholm, from 1 November 1999. Rule 13 of the special provisions of the tenancy agreement stipulated the following: “The tenant undertakes not to erect, without specific permission, placards, signs, sunblinds, outdoor aerials and such like on the house.” The agreement further stipulated, as a general condition, that the tenants were obliged to take proper care of the flat and to maintain good sanitary conditions, order and good practice.

The applicants rented a flat in Rinkeby, a suburb of Stockholm. There was a satellite dish mounted on the façade, next to one of the windows of the flat. The applicants made use of this in order to receive television programmes in Arabic and Farsi. In October 2003 the applicants' landlord changed. The new landlord, a real-estate company, demanded that the satellite dish be dismantled and, by letter of 2 April 2004, the company gave the applicants notice of termination of the tenancy agreement with effect from 31 July 2004.Shortly after having received the notice of terminate, the applicants dismantled the satellite dishes and installed a new device by placing on the kitchen floor an iron stand.

Tenants' Association found that the installation was safe and did not damage the house. The Board found that this did not involve a breach of Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. It also found that, with regard to the general obligation to maintain good sanitary conditions, order and good practice in the house, the Board considered that the actual installation did not and could not damaged the home. The new installation was, they claimed, in conformity with the rules of the tenants' tenancy agreement and it was in compliance with the law. But the Board noted that the assessment of whether tenants had failed to comply with their obligations by mounting satellite dishes had to involve the balancing of the interests of the tenant and the landlord.

Tenants' Association asked that the dish be fixed between the stand and the window. Landlord argued that the installation was safe and did not damage the house. The Board found that the fact that the new satellite installation extended through a window did not involve a breach of Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. But the Board noted that the. assessment of whether tenants had failed to comply with their obligations by mounting satellite dishes had to involve the balancing of. the interests of the tenants in using a satellite dish – which could also vary depending on. whether there were alternative means of receiving the television channels in question. The decision was made to uphold the right of tenants to have access to the TV channels.

Landlords mounted satellite dishes for reception of TV programmes. Tenants claimed they were exercising their freedom to receive information. The Tenants' Association asked that a steel wire be fixed between the dish and the stand. The Board found that the actual installation did not and could not damage the house. It also ruled that the liability for damage to persons and property could not reasonably be incurred unless it were able to prevent it. The decision was made in favour of the tenants on 21 October 2004. The appeal was dismissed on 25 January 2005 by the European Court of Human Rights. Landlord refused to let the applicants stay in their flat if they removed the satellite dish. Court found that the dish was virtually always positioned outside the kitchen window and thus constituted a permanent installation. They were given a respite until 31 March 2006 to move from the flat. They did not agree to do this and instead moved to Västerås, 110 km west of Stockholm, in June 2006. They have stated that, largely because of the scarcity of flats for rent in the Stockholm area but also due to there being a court eviction order against them, they were forced to move. The applicants had been fully aware of the importance that the landlord attached to the issue of the placement of satellite dishes and of the consequences that could follow from a refusal to comply.

Chief Justice Finlay ruled that the High Court had incorrectly construed section 6A of the 1964 Act. He considered that the Act only gave the natural father a right to apply to be guardian. It did not equate his position with that of a married father. The first and paramount consideration in the exercise of the court’s discretion was the welfare of the child, and the blood link between child and father as merely one of the many relevant factors which may be viewed by the court as relevant to that question. “Although there may be rights of interest or concern arising from the blood links between the father and the child,. there is no constitutional right to guardianship in the father of. placed for adoption.“

The Supreme Court ruled in favour of the prospective adopters in the case of V.C. against the adoption of a baby boy by his father. At about 6.30 p.m., a vehicle pulled up outside and a fourth man arrived. It appears that a bomb containing 300 to 400 pounds of explosives was prepared in the yard of the house. The digger was driven out of the yard and the other vehicle left shortly afterwards. Mr Bogusław Kijowski alleged that the domestic authorities had failed to take effective steps to enforce his right to respect for his family life in respect of his two sons. He claimed that his son A had been neglected and that he had acted in the best interests of his son. The Government submitted that the child's psychological problems had been caused by the trauma of being kidnapped by his father. The applicant was granted legal aid and was represented by a lawyer practising in Krakow. Kraków Regional Court granted the applicant's petition for divorce on 30 June 2006. The court also allowed the applicant contact rights in respect of both his sons. The applicant failed to comply with this decision and refused to return A to his mother. On 8 March 2007 the applicant was arrested and charged with paternity of his younger son B. The application was dismissed on 22 March 2005 after DNA tests were carried out. The appeal by the applicant against the judgment was dismissed on 28 December 2006 by the Krakow Court of Appeal. The reasoned judgment was notified to the applicant on 15 February 2007. The ruling was based on the reasoning of the Regional Court judgment of 30June 2006 (see paragraph 16 below) The applicant and his mother were found guilty of keeping A with them, in breach of domestic decisions. The child ran away from his mother's house and went to his father's house. On 1 April 2008 A ran away again and joined his father in Kraków. They have been living together since then. Krakow Regional Court quashed that judgment on 4 December 2009. It appears that the proceedings are pending before the trial court. The applicant is currently in pre-trial detention for six months and was released in September 2007. The court guardian visited the applicant and A. According to her opinion, A did not want to live with his mother, had good living conditions with his father and paternal grandmother. The court established that A had had de facto residence with the applicant between August 2003 and March 2007 and since April 2008. However, the court did not consider that there was enough evidence to issue an interim order changing the earlier decision of A's place of residence before the case was ready for a decision on the merits. An appeal by the applicant against this decision was dismissed on 20 July 2009. On 15 February 2010 the Kraków District Court allowed the applicant's request of 8 April 2008, granted him full parental responsibility and ordered A's return to his mother's home. The opinion was finally submitted to the court on 16 December 2009. According to the experts the best interests of A required that the residence order be changed. The court found that the applicant had never wanted his second child, contested his paternity of him and had seen B only twice: once after B's birth in 2003 and once in connection with the preparation of a psychological opinion at the RODK. In consequence B, seven years old, had not developed any emotional ties with the applicant, and in fact was afraid of him. The court concluded that the best interests of the child required all contact between him and the applicant to cease. A further appeal against the latter decision was dismissed on 20 July 2010 by the Tarnów Regional Court.

The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in Szczecin, Poland. The court acknowledged that the applicant had suffered moral damage as a result of the illegal actions of the state agents and awarded him compensation. The Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s allegations that the incident had caused a spinal injuries and dismissed the remainder of his claims for compensation.

Four men were discharged on the sole ground of sexual orientation. The High Court dismissed the application for judicial review. Lord Justice Simon Brown gave the main judgment of the court. In his view, the tide of history was against the Ministry of Defence. He further observed that it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer and added, “I doubt whether most of those present in court throughout the proceedings now believe otherwise.” However, having considered arguments as to the test to be applied in the context of these judicial review proceedings, he concluded that the conventional Wednesbury principles, adapted to a human rights context, should be applied.

The first applicant joined the Royal Navy Reserve as a radio operator in 1982. In 1994 the applicant attained the rank of lieutenant-commander. The applicant admitted to his commanding officer that he was homosexual. He was asked, inter alia, whether he had had homosexual contact with service personnel (at least four questions on this subject) He was also asked about his current relationship and whether his parents knew of his homosexuality. The application was rejected on the grounds that it did not provide sufficient proof of the applicant's sexual orientation. The case was heard by the Royal Court of Arbitration in London in 1994. The final decision was made on 13 June 1994. The second applicant joined the Royal Navy, enlisting for twenty-two years’ service. In 1991 he became a substantive weapons engineering mechanic. On 16 December 1994 the Admiralty Board informed the applicant that it had decided to terminate his commission and to discharge him, administratively, from the navy with effect from 17 January 1995. The ground for his discharge was his sexual orientation. The applicant’s commission was removed and most of the bonus which he had received with that promotion was recouped by the naval authorities (£4,875 out of £6,000). His term of service would otherwise have terminated in 2009, with the possibility of renewal. The applicant’s report dated 27 November 1992 noted that he displayed potential in a number of areas essential to good leadership. If he applied his new skills wisely he could, with experience, be considered as a potential officer candidate. In May 1993 the applicant had been refused time off to deal with a personal matter (he wished to collect his Aids test results) and consequently he spoke with the chaplain, to whom he admitted his sexual orientation. He was then called for interview by the service police. The applicant immediately confirmed his homosexuality, later clarifying that he first had “niggling doubts” about hissexual orientation approximately two and a half years previously. The applicant was discharged on the basis of his homosexuality on 28 July 1993. He was asked about gay bars he frequented, whether he had ever joined contact magazines, whether his parents knew about his homosexuality and whether he agreed that his secret life could be used as a basis to blackmail him. He further observed that it was improbable, whatever the High Court would say, that the policy could survive for much longer and added, “I doubt whether most of those present in court throughout the proceedings now believe otherwise.” But he concluded that the conventional Wednesbury principles, adapted to a human rights context, should be applied. After his conviction, Mr Maxwell instructed a new firm of solicitors, who then asked counsel who had represented him at the trial to advise on the prospects of an appeal. Having received counsel’s advice, the solicitors informed the applicant that they could not identify any basis for an appeal and accordingly could not act for him. The Court found that the appeal had not been made on the basis of the law, but that the State was liable to the extent of its responsibility.

The Supreme Court of Ireland heard the case for and against the State in 2006. The case concerned the liability of the state in relation to the acts of L.H. and L.P. of the Church of Ireland. The State paid for the system of national schools but left the decision-making to the Church. The Supreme Court ruled that the State was not liable for the actions of the church, but rather the decisions of the public. The Court of Appeal found that the state was not responsible for the acts, but the public had a right to know what was happening to the state. The Irish Free State was established in 1922. It had a largely clerically administered system of schools. The provision of free primary education was brought in by the 1998 Act. But the Act did not give the Ministers the power to make changes to the way schools were run or to appoint teachers, as they have done in the past. The Irish Free State was established to provide free education for all children. It also provided for free health care for children and the right to education for adults. It was funded by the State, not by local communities. The Irish Free State was founded on the principles of a ‘free education’ for all.

The Irish Free State had a largely clerically run system of primary schools. Most were under the control of Catholic patrons and managers, a few were under other denominations. The provision of free primary education was brought in by the Act of 1998. But it was at least partially funded by an Act of Parliament, and not by the Catholic Church. As a result, the role of the Church in primary education has been reduced to that of a ‘managerial’ role. It was the Church that was responsible for the ‘inherited tradition of managerial rights of schooling’. The Act of 1898 provided for the State to set up a system of public schools, but not for the direct control of individual teachers.

The Irish Free State was formed in 1922. It had to be run by Catholic managers. As a result, there were 3,000 schools across the country. These were all under the control of the Catholic Church. The Constitution was later amended to allow for free primary education. This has led to the current system being set up in the first place. However, it is not yet fully in place, and can only be fully implemented in the future, according to the High Court’s decision in the case of the School of Education (Ireland) vs. The Catholic Church, 2nd of May, 2013, 1st of July, 3rd of June, 2013.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 35810/09) against Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Ms Louise O’Keeffe (“the applicant”) complained under Article 3 that the system of primary education had failed to protect her from sexual abuse by a teacher in 1973. She also complained of the length of her civil proceedings and of the absence of an effective domestic remedy in that respect. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court. On 26 June 2012 a Chamber of that Section (composed of Dean Spielmann, President, Mark Villiger, Karel Jungwiert, Boštjan M. Zupančič, Ganna Yudkivska, André Potocki, judges, Peter Charleton, ad hoc judge) examined the case. The applicant attended Dunderrow National School from 1968. The school was owned, through trustees, by the Catholic Bishop of the Diocese of Cork and Ross. The manager (S.), acting on behalf of the bishop, was the local parish priest. The term “manager” used below refers both to Ó. and to the management function he performed. The applicant and the Government each filed further observations (Rule 59 § 1) on the merits. The Irish Human Rights Commission and the European Centre for Law and Justice had been given leave by the President of the Chamber to intervene in the written procedure and their submissions to the Chamber were admitted to the Grand Chamber file. In 1971 a parent of a child complained to the manager that L.H. had sexually abused her child. That complaint was not reported to the police, to the Department or to any other State authority and was not acted upon by the manager. In September 1973 other parents brought to the applicant’s parents’ attention similar allegations. The applicant suppressed the sexual abuse. In 1996 she was contacted by the police who were investigating a complaint made in 1995 by a former pupil of Dunderrow National School against L. H. L. was charged with 386 criminal offences of sexual abuse involving some twenty-one former pupils of the school. L.H. pleaded guilty to twenty-one sample charges and was sentenced to imprisonment. His licence to teach was withdrawn by the Minister for Education (‘the Minister’) under Rule 108 of the National School Rules 1965 (“the 1965 Rules”) The applicant accepted the offer by letter of 5 November 2002 and gave the standard undertaking to repay the CICT award from any other award she may receive, from whatever source, in relation to the same injury. The award was made on an ex gratia basis. Since the State is never a party to CICT proceedings, it became aware of this award later before the High Court (see directly below) Since L.H. did not file a defence, on 8 November 1999 the applicant obtained judgment in default against him. On 24 October 2006 the High Court assessed and awarded damages in the sum of EUR 305,104. The first payment was received in November 2007 so that she has been paid in the region of EUR 31,000 to date. She registered a judgment mortgage against that part of the family home owned by L.h. The applicant took enforcement proceedings. She requested a Professor Ferguson to advise her on the question of the adequacy of child-protection mechanisms in Ireland in the 1970s. Professor Ferguson agreed that, if the child- protection protocols existing in 2003 had been in place in 1973, it was very likely that the applicant’s abuse would have been acted upon in a manner which would have ensured the promotion of her welfare. The High Court accepted the State Defendants’ application on 9 March 2004. On 20 January 2006 the High Court delivered judgment. It found that the action was not statute barred. It also concluded that the State was not vicariously liable for the sexual assaults perpetrated by L.H. given the relationship between the State and the denominational management of national schools. In May 2006 the applicant appealed to the Supreme Court. Her Notice of Appeal challenged the finding on vicarious liability. By a majority judgment of 19 December 2008 (Hardiman J and Fennelly J, with whom Chief Justice Murray and Mr Justice. Mr Justice Fenna) the appeal was dismissed. The costs of the proceedings were awarded against the applicant. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal in a landmark case in 1831. The case was about the legal status of Irish national schools. The dissenting churches and the Catholic Church wished to ensure that children of their denominations be educated in schools controlled by the denomination and not by the State. Those churches were “remarkably successful’ in achieving this aim. State authorities paid for the system of national education but did not manage it or administer it at the point of delivery. The latter function was left to the local denominational manager. While State funding was accorded on a proportionate basis to all denominational schools, the population was at the time overwhelmingly Catholic so that the majority of national schools had Catholic patrons. Hardiman J referred to the “urgent desire” of the denominations to maintain their role in primary education. Most were under the control of Catholic patrons and managers. As a result there were approximately 3,000 national schools in Ireland. The provision of education was belatedly and at least partially placed on a statutory basis by the Education Act 1998. Prior to that Act the system had been administered by the 1965 Rules as well as by other ministerial letters, circulars and notes. The Minister laid down rules for national schools but they were general in nature and did not allow him to govern the detailed activities of any individual teacher. Hardiman J concluded that, having regard to the relevant test for vicarious liability and to the above-described arrangements for the control and management of national schools, the State Defendants were not liable to the applicant for the wrongs committed against her. The relationship of L.H. and the State – a “triangular one with the Church’ – was entirely sui generis and a product of Ireland’s unique historical experience. The manager was “the nominee of the patron, that is of a power other than the Minister and he did not inform the Minister of any difficulties with, or complaints about, [L.H.]” He was the agent not of the Minister, but of the Catholic Church. Hardiman J said the Minister was simply providing assistance and subvention to private and corporate (i.e. Roman Catholic) endeavour, leaving the running of the school to the private or corporate entities. Kenny J pointed out in Crowley v Ireland [1980] I.R. 102, that the Minister is deprived of the control of education by the interposing of the patron and the manager between him and the children. These persons, and particularly the latter, are in much closer and more frequent contact with the school than the Minister or the Department. The Minister can hardly be responsible for a failure to ‘cease’ a course of action of whose existence he was quite unaware’ Fennelly J accepted the expert’s evidence that it was not a State system but rather a ‘State-supported system’ He noted the clear division of power between the State (funding and fixing the curriculum) and the manager (day-to-day running of the school including hiring and firing teachers) The different religions were determined to preserve and guard their own distinct religious education so that national schools developed on a denominational basis. He concluded that the State was not vicariously liable for the acts of L.H. or for the failure of the manager to report the 1971 complaint. Geoghegan J dissented. He accepted that neither the Department nor its inspectors had any knowledge of the assaults. The applicant was legally represented throughout the civil proceedings, although she did not have legal aid. Geoghegan J relied, notably, on the role of school inspectors. If an allegation of sexual assault by a teacher on a national-school pupil was considered well-founded by an inquiry set up by the Department, it could lead to the withdrawal of recognition or to a police investigation. By a judgment of 9 May 2009 the Supreme Court vacated the High Court order for costs against the applicant since it was not disputed that hers was an important and complex test case. It determined that each party had to bear its own costs related to the action against the State Defendants.

The applicant had requested an adjournment to await the judgment of the Federal Court of Justice in the appeal proceedings brought by one of the co-defendants. The court, however, had prejudged the Federal court’s decision by holding that the plea alleging a breach of substantive law again provided nothing to support the hypothesis of an acquittal. The Hamm Court of Appeal dismissed the action on 14 July 1982. It left open the question whether, in the event of a defendant’s death before the final conclusion (rechtskräftiger Abschluss) of criminal proceedings, a decision such as that sought by Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff could be taken, by analogy, under Article 467 § 1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act (see paragraphs 24-26 below) The appeal was dismissed by the Federal Court of Justice on 11 June 1982. Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff then applied to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht), claiming a breach of the Basic Law. On 30 September 1982, a bench of three judges of the Constitutional Court refused to entertain the constitutional complaint. The reasons for its decision were as follows: “The presumption of innocence, which is founded on the principle of the rule of law, precludes treating as guilty a person who has not been finally (rechtskräftig) convicted” The decision on the claim for compensation is based on section 6(1)(2) of the Criminal Proceedings (Compensation) Act. The judge found that a conviction would have been more likely than an acquittal if the proceedings had been continued. He said this was not arbitrary in nature and did not offend the presumption of innocence. The judge also said that the judge's decision was not untenable as a result of the alleged defects in the judgment convicting the defendant and the grounds of the appeal on points of law. He added that it was the only relevant issue for the order as to costs. the proceedings were to be continued. The courts’ reference to the lack of success of. the appeal proceedings instituted by the co-defendant M and to the withdrawal of the appeals on points. of law entered by the other defendants is clearly to be regarded as an additional argument, and the impugned decisions are not based on it.

On 9 November 2000 the public prosecutor at the Diyarbakır State Security Court filed an indictment against the applicant. He accused the applicant of membership of an armed illegal organisation and of involvement in activities which undermined the constitutional order of the State. Subsequently, on 30 October 2000 the applicant was further examined at a health clinic. The Forensic Medicine Institute examined the applicant and found his allegations unsubstantiated. The applicant’s appeal was rejected on 26 June 2009 and he lost his appeal against the decision not to prosecute him. The judge ruled that the applicant had resisted the officers during his arrest and that he was making false allegations for fear of reprimand from Hizbullah members for giving evidence about the activities of the illegal organisation. The court also ruled that it was not possible to give a medical opinion on the bruises observed by the judges during the hearing of 30 November 2000, as they had not been noted in any medical report. The case was heard at the Siverek Assize Court. The case was dismissed by the court on February 4, 2013. The hearing was adjourned until April 17, 2013, when it was re-opened. The verdict was returned in favor of the defendant, who was sentenced to five years in prison. The trial was dismissed on February 5, 2013 and the sentence was suspended for five years. The appeal was dismissed in April 2013, and the conviction was overturned on April 15, 2014. The conviction was upheld on appeal on April 24, 2014, and was upheld by the Court of Appeal on April 29, 2014 on the grounds of diminished responsibility.

In 1994 it was discovered that he was infected with the HIV virus and had transmitted the virus to a 19-year-old man with whom he had first had sexual contact in 1990. It appears to be in dispute whether the instructions were included in the applicant's medical record as prescribed by section 16 of the 1988 Act. It is not in dispute, however, that the applicant was informed of the instructions, which were issued to him on 1 September 1994, both orally and in writing. The applicant kept three appointments with the county medical officer in September 1994 and one in November 1994. He failed to appear as summoned five times during October and November 1994 and was ordered to be kept in compulsory isolation in a hospital for up to three months. He is prohibited from giving blood and donating organs or sperm. Finally, he is to visit his consulting physician again and to keep appointments fixed by the countymedical officer. The County Administrative Court ordered that the applicant should be kept in compulsory isolation for up to three months pursuant to section 38 of the 1988 Act. The order took effect immediately, but the applicant failed to report to the hospital; the police accordingly took him there on 16 March 1995. The applicant absconded from the hospital several times, first on 25 April 1995. On 27 September 1995 he ran away again and was at large until the police found him on 28 May 1996. He ran away for a fourth time on 26 February 1997 and was not returned until 26 February 1999. During the period from 26 February until 2 March 1999 the applicant was detained in his room. The owner of the farm hostel gave evidence on the applicant's behalf. The applicant had drunk approximately six strong beers a week and never got drunk. He dreamt of living on his own in a flat, supporting himself on sickness benefit. He had lost all sexual desire and would in future have to decline all sexual relations. If he were to be exempted from compulsory isolation he would follow the instructions issued by the county medical officer. The most recent laboratory test, carried out on 18 March 1999, indicated that the applicant had a healthy liver. It was noted that subsequent to his return the. applicant returned to Sweden under a pseudonym. A statement was submitted to the court by a consulting psychiatric chief physician, P.N., connected to the special care facility at the hospital to which the applicant had been admitted. After the applicant's involuntary return, the chief physician had attempted to establish contact with him three times, but in vain. He claimed that on the latest occasion, in March 1999, the applicant made a lunge at him. The county medical officer, who gave evidence before the court, is recorded, inter alia, as follows: “During the last two years when he was on the run, [the applicant] sought medical treatment twice and it has been established that both times he said that he had the HIV virus’. The County Administrative Court delivered its judgment, finding against the applicant for the following reasons: “[The applicant] is HIV-positive and thus carries the HIV infection. He has been subjected to compulsory isolation since February 1995 and has during this period absconded from the hospital on several occasions – on the latest occasion for more than two years. During these two years he has used a false name and has been living a very secluded life, obviously owing to the risk of being discovered. A life at liberty makes great demands upon the person carrying the infection.” “In conclusion, in the county medical officer's opinion, [if released the applicant] will not voluntarily comply with the instructions given or limit the spreading of the disease” The Court finds that there is good reason to suppose that, if he remains free, [the applicant] will not comply with the practical instructions issued. This entails a risk of the infection spreading. The Court has not been convinced that [ the applicant] is not misusing alcohol. The applicant is likely to be unable to control his sexual behaviour. The applicants alleged that their detention ordered by the magistrates for failure to pay local taxes or court-imposed fines were unlawful. They also complained that they were not offered legal representation and were not represented at the hearing at which they were sentenced to a term of imprisonment. By a decision of 21 October 2003, the Court declared admissible the claims under Article 5 of the applicant Beet. The remainder of the applicants’ complaints were declared inadmissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. Each applicant failed to pay sums due in respect of either local taxes (community charge or council tax), or court-imposed fines. In respect of the failure to pay local taxes, the magistrates’ court had in each case determined that the applicant was liable to pay (issuing a “liability order”) In fines cases, the court had imposed the fine as the sentence following a criminal conviction. Legal aid (free legal representation where the applicant did not have sufficient means to pay for it) was not available for these enforcement proceedings prior to 1 June 1997. None of the applicants was legally represented at the hearings in front of the magistrate. The applicant’s proceedings before the magistrates arose in respect of her arrears in payment of the community charge and took place after 1 June 1997. She spent a total of 2 days in prison. The orders of the magistrate were quashed by the High Court as a result of a consent order in which it was agreed that: “(i) The decision of the justices that the applicant had culpably neglected to pay her community charge without having conducted a proper inquiry into her circumstances as of the time that the liability became due was unlawful, see R. v. Leeds Justices ex parte Kennett [1996] RVR 53.” In respect of the applicant and [her] detention, and the period of detention served, all parties agreed that the matter be remitted back to the mag Magistrates. It was agreed that costs be borne by the respondent justices see R. v. Newcastle upon Tyne Justices ex parte Devine [1998] RA 97. was further agreed that: “... in view of the fact that the Hull Justices had acknowledged the same ground in quashing the committal in R.v. Shawcross (CO/265/98), the costs of this case should also be borne.”. The decision was upheld by the Court of Appeal and the appeal was dismissed on appeal. The case was settled in the Supreme Court of England and Wales, and the verdict was quashed.

eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 9 July 1997. It originated in an application (no. 22954/93) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention and Article 3 of Protocol No. 1. On 27 August 1997, in the presence of the Registrar, the President of the Court, Mr R. Ryssdal, drew by lot the names of the other seven members of the Chamber. Liberty, a non-governmental organisation based in London, was granted leave to submit written comments on the case. These were received on 12 January 1998 and subsequently communicated to the Agent of the Government, the representative of the applicants and the Delegate of the Commission for possible observations. No observations were submitted. The Government’s responses to the applicants’ claims were filed with the registry on 21 April and 18 May 1998. The applicants filed observations in reply on 29 May 1998 and the hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 April 1998. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr C. Whomersley, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr J. Morris QC, Attorney-General and Mr J J. Eadie, Barrister-at-Law, Counsel. The history of the enactment of the relevant measures as well as their purport and scope are described in Section B below. The impact of the measures on the applicants, all persons considered holders of politically restricted posts within the meaning of the applicable legislation, is described in sections C and D. The adoption of the Local Government Officers (Political Restrictions) Regulations 1990 is explained in Section C below. Section D describes the effect of the regulations on the role of local government officials in the political process, such as the involvement of certain categories of officials in political activities. The regulations are intended to combat the politicisation of the local government system. The Local Government Officers (Political Restrictions) Regulations 1990 (“the Regulations”) were made under section 1(5) of the Act on 4 April 1990. They were laid before Parliament the following day and came into force on 1 May 1990. The Regulations applied to all persons holding a politically restricted post. This term covers three broad categories of local government officials: the most senior post-holders in the local authorities, and those who have been councillors for the last year. The regulations make it illegal for officers at the rank of principal officer and above to hold office in a political party. They also ban them from speaking or writing in public in a way that might be regarded as engaging in party political debate. Local government officials in the first and second categories were deemed to be subject to the Regulations. An officer in the second and third categories could apply to an independent adjudicator to have his or her post removed from the list of posts to which the Regulations applied (section 3) The first applicant, Mr Ahmed, was a solicitor employed by the London Borough of Hackney. Mr Perrin was Principal Valuer with the Devon County Council (a category three officer). He was responsible for leading, leading the Housing Benefits Review Board. Mr Ahmed was adopted as Labour candidate for election to the London borough of Enfield in 1990, but was obliged to withdraw his candidature as a result of the regulations. Mr Perrin's post required him to give regular advice to the Council’s committees, including strategy advice on key estate management issues. Mr Perrin applied for exemption from political restrictions on the ground that although he advised the Council and spoke to the media, the advice was ‘factual valuation information regarding the acquisition, disposal and management of property’ His application for exemption was refused on 20 March 1990. Mr Bentley's post was classified as one that was politically sensitive (a category one post) and appropriately subject to political restrictions under section 2(3) of the Act. He was also restricted in canvassing for his wife who stood as the only Labour Councillor for the West Devon Borough Council, and in giving radio interviews. Mr Bentley applied for exemption from political restrictions. Mr Brough is employed by the Hillingdon Borough Council as the head of its Committee Services Department. He can no longer act as Parliamentary Chairman of his party in Harrow East and is prevented from speaking at public meetings on issues such as housing and the health service. Judicial review proceedings challenging the validity of the Regulations were dismissed. The applicants and NALGO (the predecessor of UNISON, the trade union of which the applicants are members and which represents public-sector workers) applied for and were granted leave to apply for judicial review of the regulations. The application was dismissed on 20 December 1991. Judge referred to an affidavit submitted by Mr Simcock, a senior civil servant at the Department of the Environment. He explained how the Widdicombe Committee had been set up in 1985 to inquire into local authority practices and procedures with particular reference to the respective roles of elected members and officers. The judge continued: “... I preface my summary by pointing out that some of [the applicants’ complaints] reflect the applicant’s root and branch opposition to the whole concept of restricting the political activities of local government employees’” NALGO was involved in the making of the Regulations, in which the judge said the regulations were in some respects less restrictive than the Committee's proposals. He added that there was no pressing social need for the Regulations. The Regulations go too far in prohibiting conduct undertaken with apparent intention, etc., or likely to create the impression of support, etc. They should, at most, have proscribed actual political activities. The width of the language used means that many non-party political activities, including trade unions and charitable activities, are prohibited. The terms are imposed on existing employees, who entered into their contracts of employment on a different basis. The restrictions may have an adverse effect on recruitment and lead to resignations by skilled staff. The arguments summarised in (c) and (d) are to the effect that the Regulations are uncertain and incapable of consistent and fair application. An appeal to the Court of Appeal was dismissed on 26 November 1992. Lord Justice Neill found that the provisions of Article 10 of the Convention did not assist NALGO and the applicants. The other judges, Lords Justices Russell and Rose, agreed. The House of Lords refused leave to appeal to it on 24 March 1993. Leave to appealed to the House of Commons was refused on 19 March 1994. The Regulations were not ‘Wednesbury unreasonable’ or ultra vires, the judge said. He also agreed with the first-instance judge as to legitimate expectation. He said that the argument mentioned in (f) is in my view misconceived.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that there had been a violation of Article 8, taken separately or together with Article 14, on account of the refusal by the national authorities to indicate her forename in the civil register of births as that of the mother of her adopted child. She argued that in relation to single-parent adoptions there was a lacuna in the Civil Code which required the court to make provision for such a situation. The court dismissed the applicant’s request on the ground that it had no legal basis. It found that the Civil Code, in choosing to regulate only two-parent adoptions, intended to treat the legal relationship between the adoptive parents and the adopted child as ‘a biological relationship’ On 14 April 2008 the applicant appealed on points of law. In March 2009 a new regulation entered into force entitled “Regulation on the implementation of mediation services for the adoption of minors’ (“the Regulation”) enabling a single adoptive parent to have his or her forename registered in the place of that of the biological parent. That request was granted on the same day and the record entries concerning the child were consequently amended with immediate effect.

The applicant, who is black, is a British citizen born in 1966 and currently living in Manchester, England. He was tried for robbery at Manchester Crown Court between 26 and 28 November 1991. On the final day of the trial, at 10.46 a.m., the jury retired to consider their verdict. An hour and three quarters later a note was passed by the judge to the judge. It read: “JURY SHOWING RACIAL OVERTONES 1 MEMBER TO BE EXCUSED.“ In the absence of the jury, the trial was held in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 October 1996. Defence counsel seems to recall that he did in fact ask the trial judge to discharge the jury in the circumstances, but his application was refused. Defence counsel based his recollection on the grounds of appeal and advice on appeal which he drafted shortly after the trial on 10 December 1991. Judge showed the note to counsel for the prosecution and defence and consulted them on the appropriate response to it. The applicant renewed his application to the full Court of Appeal. On 19 January 1993 the application was dismissed. The jury system does require an element of give and take after proper directions from the judge. A member of the jury felt that there was a general overtone of racial comment which was unacceptable and not, as the applicant is suggesting, so racially prejudiced as to be unable to give proper consideration to the matters before him. The right to silence is part of the Constitution. The right to remain silent is meant to protect the right to freedom of speech. It is intended to provide for the protection of the right of the public to know the identity of those who have committed an act of terrorism or of any other criminal offence. It does not mean that the public must be aware of the identities of those that have committed a crime in the past or that they have committed any offence in the future. The Constitutional Court found no indication that the members of the Regional Appeals Commission lacked independence or impartiality. “It is true that the assessors ... are representatives of two conflicting spheres of interest. These members are not bound by instructions from the sending organisation ... and they are by no means spokespersons of these organisations,” the court said. ‘A violation of the required impartiality could, thus, ... be due to specific circumstances in the individual case resulting, for example, from an official or organisational dependence of the appointed member,’ it added. The court concluded: ‘‘A constellation affecting the appearance of independence and impartiality’ could only exist if the appointed assessors had been involved in the preparation of the general agreement or if there were other specific reasons raising legitimate doubts about their independence’

The Austrian Agricultural Market Act (Agrarmarkt) requires the company to pay a fee for every animal slaughtered. The company was ordered to pay an amount of 11.730,05 euros in unpaid contributions in December 2005 and January 2006. It appealed against the order, saying it was contrary to the rules of the European Union on state aid. The Federal Minister of Agriculture, Forestry, Environment and Water decided not to hold a hearing on the appeal. He said it was in accordance with the law that the contributions were to be made in line with the European Community's Common Market rules. The appeal was dismissed on 17 July 2006, and a new payment order was made.

The Federal Minister of Agriculture, Forestry, Environment and Water, acting as the appeal authority, refused to hold a hearing. The European Commission said that the payments were in accordance with EU law. The Federal Minister said that there was no need for a hearing because the payment was made in line with the rules of the European Community. The Court ruled in favour of the company and ordered the payment to be made in full. The company was forced to pay a surcharge of 60% of the unpaid contributions. The case was heard on 17 July 2006, and the decision was upheld by the Court of Appeal on 17 August 2006. The judge ruled that the payment of the surcharge to the company was not in breach of EU law, but that it was in violation of an agreement to make the payment.

The Austrian government ordered the company to pay back money. The company appealed against the order. It argued that the order was contrary to the rules of the European Union on state aid. The case was dismissed on 17 July 2006, and no further action was taken against the company. The Court of Appeal ruled that the payment was in accordance with EU law. The decision was based on the European Commission’s decision of 30 June 2004 (C(2004)2037), which said that the company had to pay the full amount owed. The Federal Minister of Agriculture, Forestry, and Wirtschaft said that it was not necessary to hold a hearing because the decision was already made by the European Council.

The court ruled that refusal to change the sex of a post-operative transsexual in the register of births was an unjustified interference with human dignity and everyone’s fundamental right to develop his personality freely. On 25 October 1996 the Federal constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant's constitutional complaint. The German health insurance system has been governed by the Social Security Act, Book V, Health Insurance (Sozialgesetzbuch, Fünftes Buch, Gesetzliche Kranken-versicherung) since 1989. Under the relevant provisions, persons insured under the health system are entitled to medical treatment which is necessary in order to diagnose or to cure a disease. The cost of gender reassignment surgery had to be reimbursed if, in the circumstances of the individual case, the psychophysical state of the transsexual amounted to a disease and if the sole means of finding relief, psychiatric and psychotherapeutic treatment had remained unsuccessful. Private health insurance covers expenses for curative treatment which is medically necessary on account of a disease or injuries suffered as a result of an accident. The insurer is exempted from liability if the insured person has deliberately caused his or her own disease or accident (section 178.l). The contractual relations are standardised in general insurance conditions. The Federal Court of Justice, in a decision of 11 April 1994 (Versicherungsrecht 1995, pp. 447 et seq.), endorsed the lower court’s finding that gender reassignment surgery had to be considered as necessary medical treatment. In its judgment of 30 April 1996 in P. v. S. and Cornwall County Council (C-13/94, Rec. 1996, p. I-2143), the ECJ found that discrimination arising from gender. reassignment constituted discrimination on grounds of sex and, accordingly, Article 5. of Council Directive 76/207/EEC of 9 February 1976. ECJ: Community law as it stands at present does not cover discrimination based on sexual orientation. ‘Discrimination based on the fact that a person belongs to a particular sex is limited to the case of a worker’s gender reassignment and does not therefore apply to differences of treatment based on a person's sexual orientation,’ it said. reasoning, which leads to the conclusion that such discrimination is to be prohibited just as is discrimination based. on sex, the court said. 'The refusal by an employer to allow travel concessions to the person of the same sex with whom a worker has a stable relationship does not constitute discrimination prohibited by Article 119 of the Treaty or Directive 75/117,' it added.

Teachers of Grieskirchen secondary school brought proceedings against the applicant for insult and damage to their reputation before the Peuersbach District Court. The court noted that, in the course of time, the atmosphere between the pupils and teachers at the Grieskin secondary school had been strained. The spokesperson of the pupils had complained that the teachers did not take her seriously and avoided any discussion about the boycott measures with her. The judge noted that the statement was an insult and a defamation within the meaning of Article 1330 of the Civil Code. It ordered the applicant to refrain from repeating the statement that teachers were applying pressure on pupils and parents to an intolerable extent and that this amounted in fact to an abuse of their authority. The court further observed that the conflicting interests of teachers, parents and pupils in regard to the boycott measures naturally caused tensions. There was, however, no indication that the teachers had used unlawful and unobjective means, such as, for example, the use of their authority to assign marks. It was, on the contrary, because of the teachers' unbending attitude that pupils and parents had finally resigned and agreed to the compromise. The Wels Regional Court dismissed the appeal. It noted that the statement at issue constituted a statement of fact susceptible of proof. The injunction at issue did, therefore, not violate the applicant's right to freedom of expression.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47709/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 18 October 1998. The applicants alleged, in particular, that they had been deprived of their liberty during an unlawful search of their apartment and that the police had used excessive and unjustified force towards them. They complained of a breach of Articles 3, 5 and 8 of the Convention. By a decision of 21 October 2008 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The parties do not fully agree about the facts of the case, which may be summarised as follows. The applicants lived in the house with the owner’s permission. They often received young visitors from all over the country. On 16 June 1997 the applicants requested to be examined by a forensic medicine specialist. It was established that the first applicant had two long bruises on his left arm, and other bruises on the palm of his hand. The second applicant had a blue mark on her bottom (13 by 9 cm) It was stated that these bruises could have been caused by the use of police truncheons. The applicants asked for a court hearing and were granted a hearing on 19 June 1997. The court ruled to acquit the applicants of any wrongdoing. The Wrocław District Prosecutor found that no criminal offence had been committed. The prosecutor considered that the police action had been justified. The police could have reasonably suspected that the unlocked car had been stolen, even though it had not been reported as such. The applicant was most probably hit once. As the applicants were interfering with the arrest of D. S., they were hit with truncheons. On 16 June 1997 the applicants requested the Wroclaw District. Prosecutor to institute criminal proceedings against the police for abuse of. authority. On 23 December 1997 the prosecutor refused to do so. The. prosecutor’s investigation and conclusion concluded that the application was not a criminal offence. D. S. had objected in a loud voice to the police intervention. He had insisted that the intention of the police was to harass the persons in the house. The prosecutor considered that this had been justified in the light of D. S’s aggressive behaviour. It was finally noted that the accounts of the facts given by the persons present at the scene, other than the police, were highly divergent. Therefore, the submissions of the other persons could not be considered credible and had to be assessed critically. The appeal against the prosecutor's decision was dismissed. The first applicant appealed. He argued that the police brutality and aggression had been totally unjustified. D. S. argued that he was a law-abiding citizen, a student of two university faculties and a member of the Municipal Council of his town. The police should not intervene in private property at night and hit, insult and humiliate people just because they looked, or lived, differently. The Wrocław Regional Prosecutor upheld the contested decision. The outcome of the appeal was not made public until after the appeal had been heard by the High Court of Justice in Strasbourg in June 1998. The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal on 8 June 1998, and D. S.'s appeal was rejected on 9 August 1998, with the decision to be made public later that month.

The first sought primarily to amend Article 10 para. 2 of the basic law; the second was designed to limit the right to secrecy of the mail,Post and telecommunications. Law guaranteed the secrecy of mail, post and telecommunications with a proviso that restrictions could be ordered only pursuant to a statute. As amended by the Act of 24 June 1968, it now provides: “(1) Secrecy of the mail,Post and telecommunications shall be inviolable. (2) Restrictions may be orderedonly pursuant to an act of parliament.” The measure may be taken to protect against “imminent dangers’ threatening the “free democratic constitutional order’, “the existence or the security of the Federation or of a Land“ and the ‘allied armed forces’ stationed on the territory of the Republic. The Act provides that surveillance measures can only be ordered by head of one of the following services: the Agencies for the Protection of the Constitution of the Federation and the Länder, the Army Security Office (Amt für Sicherheit der Bundeswehr) and the Federal Intelligence Service (Bundesnachrichtendienst) The measures are ordered, on written application giving reasons, either by the supreme Land authority in cases falling within its jurisdiction or by a Federal Minister empowered for the purpose by the Chancellor. Measures ordered must be immediately discontinued once the required conditions have ceased to exist or the measures themselves are no longer necessary. The measures remain in force for a maximum of three months and may be renewed only on fresh application. The G 10 Commission decides, ex officio or on application by a person believing himself to be under surveillance, on both the legality of and the necessity for the measures. If it declares any measures to be illegal or unnecessary, the Minister must terminate them immediately. The Commission members are appointed for the current term of the Bundestag by the above-mentioned Board of five Members of Parliament after consultation with the Government. They are completely independent in the exercise of their functions and cannot be subject to instructions. The Government, moreover, intend proposing to Parliament to amend the G 10 so as to make such prior consent obligatory. The G 10 commission draws up its own rules of procedure which must be approved by the Board. The surveillance of the post and telecommunications of a certain person can serve a useful purpose only if the person concerned does not become aware of it. For this reason, notification to this person is out of the question. For the same reason, it must be avoided that a person who intends to commit, or who has committed, the offences enumerated in the Act can, by using a legal remedy, inform himself whether he is under surveillance. The Bill presented during the 4th legislative session ... provided for the ordering (of such measures) by an independent judge. The Federal Government abandoned this solution in the Bill amending Article 10 of the Basic Law, introduced as part of the Emergency Legislation. If the person concerned is notified, after the measures have been discontinued, that he has been subject to surveillance, several legal remedies against the interference with his rights become available to him. The authorities are bound to reply to such a request even if the information asked for is secret. It is then for the Constitutional Court to decide whether the information and documents so obtained can be used. The latter may reject the application on the ground that the applicant is unable to adduce proof to substantiate a complaint, but it may also request the Government concerned to supply it with information or to produce documents to enable it to verify for itself the individual’s allegations. The applicants alleged that Article 10 para. 2 of the Basic Law and the G 10 violate Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention. On 18 December 1974, the Commission declared the application admissible. In view of this particularity of the case the applicants have to be considered as victims for the purpose of Article 25 (art. 25) of the convention. The Commission then expressed the opinion:by eleven votes to one with two abstentions, that the present case did not disclose any breach of Article 6 para. 1 ( art. 6-1) The applicants relied on the notion “civil rights’;. The case did not disclose any breach of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) in so far as the applicants relied on the notion “criminal charge’. The report contains various separate opinions. The applicants could claim to be ‘victims’ of a violation of their rights guaranteed by the Convention by reason of the system of surveillance established by the so-called G 10 Act;. Background to the case is as follows: Gerhard Schröder called a vote of confidence in the Federal Chancellor on 1 July 2005 and lost it. None of the main political parties emerged victorious with a sufficient majority, but the parties forming the SPD and the Greens lost their majority.
